INTRODUCTION

Why knowing a rule on paper is different from owning it in speech

Most English learners have had the same frustrating experience. You study a grammar rule, you complete a page of exercises without a single mistake, and you feel ready. Then someone asks you an unexpected question in a real conversation — and in that split second, the rule disappears. You hesitate, translate in your head, or fall back on the same safe, simple sentences you were using two years ago.

That gap between what you recognize on paper and what you can say out loud is not a lack of intelligence or effort. It happens because most grammar books teach grammar as a set of abstract formulas for your eyes, whereas speaking requires fast, meaningful choices in your voice.

In real life, grammar is not decoration. It is how you signal what you mean. The difference between 'I lived in Herat for three years' and 'I have lived in Herat for three years' tells your listener whether you still live there today. The difference between 'You mustn't be late' and 'He can't be late' separates a strict rule from a logical guess. When you understand what a structure actually does for your listener, you stop memorizing charts and start making clear, confident choices.

This book is built around one simple habit: speak first, see the principle clearly, hear the difference, and immediately use the pattern in real conversation. Every small improvement in how you connect tenses, frame questions, compare ideas, or soften a claim compounds over time. Fix one recurring habit in each lesson, and within sixteen lessons your spoken English sounds noticeably clearer, more natural, and more persuasive.

By the end of this course, you will be able to:

• choose the right tense to describe habits, ongoing projects, past stories, and life changes;

• ask natural questions, soften polite requests, and keep a real conversation moving;

• express advice, certainty, possibilities, wishes, and regrets with the exact shade of meaning you intend;

• compare options persuadably and connect your ideas into clear, logical arguments;

• shift focus smoothly using the passive voice, causative patterns, relative clauses, and participles;

• report what others said accurately and control your tone with hedging and natural emphasis;

• catch and repair your own slips in the middle of a conversation without losing your flow.

HOW TO USE THIS BOOK

A practical guide to turning grammar into automatic speech

Four habits that make this book work

1. Always speak before you read the rule. Every lesson begins with The Speaking Hook — a short situation or question to discuss with a partner right away. Do not worry about perfection in those first two minutes. Speaking first wakes up your ear; when you read The Simple Rule a moment later, you will immediately recognize the exact tool you were just reaching for.

2. Read the side-by-side contrasts aloud. In See the Difference, you will see pairs of sentences that look similar on the page but send very different messages in conversation. Say both sentences out loud and notice where your voice stresses the words. Your ear remembers contrasts far better than definitions.

3. Stretch your answers to match your voice. Everyone in your class works through the same lessons and conversations together. In every speaking activity, start by making your core point clearly and accurately. Once that feels comfortable, push yourself one step further: add a concrete example, explain the reason behind your choice, address another point of view, or try one of the sharper patterns in Part 6 (Say It with Greater Precision).

4. Close the book for the final recall check. At the end of every lesson, cover the page and answer the retrieval prompts out loud from memory. Calling a pattern up from memory without looking at the page is what moves grammar from short-term recognition into long-term speech.

DIAGNOSTIC TEST

Find your starting point — 25 questions · no time limit

Complete this test before Lesson 1 without studying first: the purpose is simply to see which patterns already feel natural and which ones deserve extra attention. Mark your score out of 25 and keep your notes. This is a broad starting snapshot, not a parallel form of the 30-item Final Assessment; do not interpret the difference between their raw totals as a learning gain. For a direct before-and-after comparison, complete the speaking sample in Part D and score it with the same four-criterion rubric used at the end of the book.

Part A — Tenses and time (10 questions)

1. I __________ (see) that film last week.

2. She __________ (work) here since 2021.

3. While I __________ (cook — ongoing background), the phone rang.

4. They __________ (work) there for ten years before they moved to Kabul.

5. At sea level, pure water __________ (boil) at 100°C.

6. They __________ (build) a new bridge when we visited.

7. I __________ my keys — I can't get in. (lose)

8. Last summer we __________ (go) to Herat.

9. How many books __________ you __________ (read) so far this month?

10. When I arrived, the train __________ already __________ (leave).

Part B — Structures (10 questions)

11. If it __________ (rain), we'll stay home.

12. I wish I __________ (know) the answer.

13. My phone needs __________. (repair)

14. The report __________ (write) by the team last week.

15. He suggested __________ early. (leave)

16. Could you tell me where __________ ? (the station / be)

17. The girl __________ helped me was very kind. (who / that / whose / which)

18. I'd rather you __________ (not, smoke) here.

19. Ali is __________ than his brother. (intelligent)

20. Not until midnight __________. (she / finish)

Part C — Use and communication (5 questions)

21. I __________ find my passport anywhere. (mustn't / can't)

22. __________ being very tired, he finished the race. (Despite / Although)

23. She asked me, "Where do you live?" → She asked me __________.

24. It __________ rain later — take an umbrella. (may / might / could)

25. I __________ my hair cut yesterday. (had / got)

Part D — Baseline speaking sample (not included in the 25-point written snapshot)

Speak for two minutes

Choose one topic. Prepare for two minutes, then speak for two minutes without reading a script:

• A decision that changed your life — and what you would do differently today.

• One change that would improve education or work in your country.

• A person who influenced you, and the advice they gave you.

After your talk, a partner asks two follow-up questions. Answer them, then ask one relevant question in return. If you get stuck, repair and continue. LESSON 1 · TENSES FOR REAL COMMUNICATION

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: talk about habits, experiences and changes accurately

Imagine two candidates in a job interview. The first says, 'I worked at a city clinic for three years.' The second says, 'I have worked at a city clinic for three years.' Only one small word changed, yet the interviewer hears two completely different life stories: the first person no longer works there, while the second still walks through those clinic doors every morning.

Tenses are not a chart of endings to memorise for a test. They are the camera lens you choose every time you open your mouth — telling your listener whether something is a permanent routine, a temporary project, a closed chapter in the past, or a change that still shapes your life today.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Read these two pairs of sentences aloud with a partner:

• 'I live with my cousin.' vs. 'I'm living with my cousin until my flat is ready.'

• 'I lost my keys yesterday.' vs. 'I've lost my keys — can you let me in?'

Without using grammar terms, explain to your partner what changes in the real-world situation between the left sentence and the right sentence. Then take one minute each to answer:

• What does a normal weekday look like for you, and what is one temporary project you are working on this month?

• What is one important thing that has changed in your daily life over the past year?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Present tenses: habits, facts and what is happening now

When you talk about the present, English asks a simple question: are you describing your normal baseline, or are you shining a spotlight on something temporary happening around now?

Use the present simple for your baseline — habits, routines, permanent facts, fixed timetables, and mental states. Use the present continuous when an action is in progress right now, when a project is temporary around this period of your life, or when a situation is gradually changing.

Pattern:

Present simple: Subject + base verb (+ s/es for he/she/it) → habits · facts · fixed timetables · states

Present continuous: Subject + am/is/are + verb-ing → happening now · current projects · temporary situations · changing trends

Natural examples:

• I work in a medical clinic, and our morning shift starts at eight. (permanent routine and fixed timetable)

• I'm working on my pronunciation this month by recording myself for five minutes a day. (temporary current project)

• More professionals are learning English online every year. (an ongoing trend)

• I know the answer, and I believe your plan will work. (mental states stay in the present simple)

Keep in mind:

→ Add -s or -es with he, she, and it in the present simple: he works, she studies, it matters.

→ Stative verbs describe a state rather than an active process (know, believe, understand, own, belong, seem, prefer). They normally stay in the simple form: say 'I understand the problem' (not 'I am understanding').

Rule 2 — Past simple vs present perfect: closed time vs connected to now

Many speakers hesitate between 'I did' and 'I have done' because both refer to something that happened before now. The real difference is not how long ago the event happened — it is whether the time period is closed or still connected to the present.

Use the past simple when you name or think of a finished time period (yesterday, last summer, in 2020, when I was a student). That chapter is closed. Use the present perfect when the time period is still open (today, this week, so far this year), when a past event has a clear result right now, or when a situation began in the past and continues up to today (often with since or for). 'Recently' can take either tense, depending on the time focus and variety of English.

Pattern:

Past simple: Subject + past verb (verb-ed / irregular) → a finished, closed time in the past

Present perfect: Subject + have/has + past participle → open time period · life experience · present result · continuing to now

Natural examples:

• I visited Bamyan last summer with my classmates. (finished time: 'last summer' is over)

• I have visited Bamyan twice in my life. (life experience up to now — no finished time is named)

• Nadia has lived in this neighbourhood since 2021. (she moved here in 2021 and still lives here today)

• I've sent the application, so we can relax now. (past action with a direct present result)

Keep in mind:

→ Once you attach a finished time stamp (yesterday, two days ago, in 2019), close the door with the past simple: 'I saw him yesterday' (never 'I have seen him yesterday').

→ With 'recently', either tense can be natural: 'I've spoken to her recently' (focusing on the recent link to now) or 'I spoke to her recently' (thinking of that specific recent occasion).

Rule 3 — Talking about changes and the future

English does not have just one future tense because we do not think about every future event in the same way. Whenever you talk about tomorrow or next year, you are showing your listener how prepared that future is.

Choose 'be going to + base verb' when you have already made a decision or plan before speaking, or when you can see clear present evidence of what is about to happen. Choose 'will + base verb' when you make an instant decision while speaking, make a promise, or state a general prediction. Choose the present continuous (with a future time expression) when you have a fixed arrangement with another person or organisation.

Pattern:

am/is/are going to + base verb → prior plans and intentions · predictions from visible evidence

will + base verb → decisions made while speaking · promises and offers · general predictions

Present continuous + future time word → fixed personal arrangements already on the calendar

Natural examples:

• I'm going to take the TOEFL exam next spring — I've already bought the study guide. (decided plan)

• Those bags look heavy — I'll carry one for you. (instant offer made at the moment of speaking)

• We're meeting the new instructor on Thursday at ten. (fixed arrangement with a specific time)

Keep in mind:

→ In future time and condition clauses starting with if, when, as soon as, before, or after, use the present simple: 'When the results arrive, I'll call you' and 'If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay indoors.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

Present perfect vs past simple — the choice is about TIME

Look at how the same verb changes meaning when you shift from the past simple to the present perfect. In each pair below, ask yourself: is the speaker looking back at a finished moment, or looking at how the past touches right now?

Past simple (closed past time)

Present perfect (connected to now)

What your listener hears

I lost my keys yesterday.

I've lost my keys.

The left sentence reports when it happened (perhaps I found them later). The right sentence is about right now: I am standing outside the door and cannot get in.

She worked at the hospital for five years.

She has worked at the hospital for five years.

Past simple means her five-year period is finished — she works somewhere else now. Present perfect means she started five years ago and still works there.

Did you eat breakfast this morning?

Have you eaten breakfast this morning?

We ask 'Did you eat?' when the morning is over. We ask 'Have you eaten?' while it is still morning and there is still time to make you some toast.

State verbs vs action verbs — when a verb changes its job

Most state verbs (know, believe, understand, belong, own, seem, prefer) describe a steady condition, so they stay in the simple form: 'I understand the rule' — never 'I am understanding the rule.'

However, a few everyday verbs have two meanings: a state meaning (simple) and an active meaning (continuous). Compare: 'I think this course is practical' (my opinion — state) versus 'I'm thinking about applying for a scholarship' (an active mental process happening right now). Likewise, 'She has a small car' (ownership) versus 'She's having lunch with her supervisor' (an action in progress).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. I __________ (see) that documentary last week, and we talked about it for hours.

2. Nadia __________ (work) at the children's hospital since 2022.

3. We __________ (meet) the new course director tomorrow morning at ten. (fixed arrangement)

4. Look out of the window — it __________ (snow)!

5. My older brother __________ (believe) that consistent daily practice beats last-minute cramming.

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Correct the mistake and explain why: 'I have finished my assignment last night.'

2. Correct the mistake and explain why: 'She is knowing three foreign languages.'

3. Choose the natural form: How long (do you know / have you known) your closest friend, Sara?

4. Rewrite using going to so it sounds like a decided plan: 'My intention is to study medicine next year.'

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Interview your partner using the four questions below. Do not treat this as a checklist — listen closely to the details in every answer and ask at least one natural follow-up question before moving to the next prompt.

• What does a typical weekend look like for you when you have no urgent deadlines?

• What is something new or different you are doing these days that was not part of your routine six months ago?

• What was the best part of your last weekend, and who were you with?

• What has changed most in your work, studies, or daily habits since last year?

How it sounds in conversation:

A: What are you doing these days that wasn't part of your routine six months ago?

B: I'm walking to class every morning instead of taking the bus. It takes forty minutes, so I listen to English podcasts on the way.

A: That's a great habit. How long have you been doing that, and have you noticed a difference in your listening?

Your conversation goal: Both partners answer all four questions, exchange at least four follow-up questions in total, and can report one interesting answer about the other person to the class.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ uses present simple for regular habits and routines

✓ uses present continuous for current projects and temporary changes

✓ uses past simple for finished past moments and present perfect for changes continuing to now

✓ asks natural follow-up questions that react to what the partner actually said

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

Once your tense choices are accurate, you can express richer shades of time by showing continuous effort, contrasting past setbacks with present growth, or highlighting a milestone.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Link every time expression directly to its natural tense: finished markers (yesterday, two weeks ago, in 2020) close the action in the past simple; open bridges (since 2021, for three months, so far this week) connect to now with the present perfect.

• Say three true sentences about your own week aloud: one permanent habit, one temporary project you are doing this month, and one experience you have had this year.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use the present perfect continuous (have/has been + verb-ing) when you want to emphasise the ongoing effort or visible effect of an activity: 'I've been revising all morning, so my eyes are tired.'

• Combine past simple and present perfect in a single sentence to show growth from a past event: 'I failed the driving test twice last year, but I've learned from both mistakes and I feel ready now.'

• Use milestone frames such as 'It's the first time I've ever…' or 'This is the most challenging project I've worked on' to highlight a standout experience.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 30 seconds to jot down three keywords only (do not write full sentences): one past turning point (past simple), one change that has happened up to now (present perfect), and one habit or focus you are working on these days (present simple / continuous).

Speak without reading: Speak for one full minute: How has your English — or another practical skill you value — improved over time? Name one specific past moment that helped you, explain what has changed since then, and describe what you are actively working on right now.

Model response — speak first, then compare

I've been studying English seriously for about two years. Last year I joined a weekly speaking club, and that was the moment things really changed for me — I learned to respond in English right away instead of translating every word in my head. Since then, my confidence has grown a lot, and I've spoken in front of visitors twice at work. These days I listen to a short news podcast every morning while I walk, and I'm focusing on making my pronunciation clearer.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ past simple used for the specific turning-point event

✓ present perfect used for progress and changes up to now

✓ present continuous used for what the speaker is focusing on these days

✓ time expressions match the chosen tenses naturally (last year, since then, these days)

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Present simple describes your permanent baseline (habits, facts, states); present continuous spotlights what is in progress or temporary around now.

• Past simple closes the door on a finished time (yesterday, in 2020); present perfect connects the past to the present moment.

• For the future, use 'going to' for decided plans, 'will' for spontaneous decisions and predictions, and the present continuous for fixed arrangements.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'I have seen him yesterday.' → 'I saw him yesterday.' (A finished time stamp requires the past simple.)

→ 'I am knowing the answer.' → 'I know the answer.' (State verbs stay in the simple form.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Describe your last weekend in four connected past-simple sentences, then add one sentence in the present perfect about how your week has gone so far.

• Explain three things that have changed in your town, work, or studies since 2020.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can talk about a routine, a current project, and a past experience in one smooth answer.

☐ I can hear the difference between a finished past event and a situation that continues up to now.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 1 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. saw · 2. has worked / has been working · 3. are meeting · 4. is snowing · 5. believes

Practice B: 1. I finished my assignment last night. ('last night' is a finished time) · 2. She knows three foreign languages. ('know' is a state verb) · 3. have you known · 4. I'm going to study medicine next year.

LESSON 2 · TELLING STORIES AND DESCRIBING EXPERIENCES

Part 1 — Build Strong Sentences | Speaking goal: tell a story with background, sequence and clear focus

Have you ever listened to someone tell a story that sounded like a flat shopping list? 'I woke up late. I ran outside. It rained. I missed the bus. My phone died.' Every sentence is grammatically correct, yet the story feels lifeless because every action is painted on the exact same flat surface.

Skilled storytellers use grammar like a film director uses cameras. One tense paints the atmosphere in the background, another drives the main events forward step by step, and a third flashes back to something that had already happened before the scene began.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Compare these two openings to the same story:

• Version A: 'I walked home from work. The lights went out. I realized my keys were on my office desk.'

• Version B: 'I was walking home from work when the street lights suddenly went out — and that was the moment I realized I had left my keys on my office desk.'

Read both versions aloud with a partner. Why does Version B pull the listener in? Then take 30 seconds each to tell a brief true story about a small surprise, delay, or lucky moment from your own life.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Past continuous: painting the background scene

Before an audience cares about what happened, they need to see where you were and what was going on around you. That is the job of the past continuous (was/were + verb-ing).

Think of the past continuous as a wide-angle background shot that is already rolling when a sudden, shorter action (in the past simple) steps into the frame: 'I was waiting at the pharmacy when my old teacher walked in.' The waiting was already in progress; the entrance interrupted or punctuated it.

Pattern:

Past continuous: Subject + was/were + verb-ing → ongoing background scene · action in progress at a past moment

Scene + interruption: While + past continuous, past simple / Past continuous + when + past simple

Natural examples:

• I was walking across the campus when I ran into an old classmate.

• A cold wind was blowing and shopkeepers were closing their shutters as we reached the market.

• While I was preparing the slides, the projector suddenly stopped working.

Keep in mind:

→ Use 'while' before the ongoing background action (past continuous) and 'when' before the shorter interrupting event (past simple): 'While I was cooking dinner, the lights went out' / 'I was cooking dinner when the lights went out.'

Rule 2 — Past perfect: stepping one level further back

Stories do not always unfold in strict 1–2–3 calendar order. Often you start your story at an exciting moment — arriving at the airport gate, opening an exam paper, meeting someone — and then you need to point back to something that happened earlier.

If you keep using the past simple, your listener thinks the events happened one after another ('When I arrived, he left' means my arrival caused him to walk out). When you switch to the past perfect (had + past participle), you signal a flashback: 'When I arrived, he had already left' (the room was already empty when I got there).

Pattern:

Past perfect: Subject + had + past participle → an action completed before another past moment

Natural examples:

• By the time we reached the cinema, the film had already started.

• She looked relieved because she had finally submitted her thesis.

• I recognized the street immediately because I had visited the neighbourhood years earlier.

Keep in mind:

→ Do not overuse the past perfect for every sentence in a story. Use it only when you jump backwards from your main past storyline to an earlier event: 'By the time the taxi arrived (main past), we had packed everything (earlier past).'

Rule 3 — Signposting the sequence and landing the ending

In written English, paragraphs show the reader how a story is organized. In spoken English, your listener cannot see paragraphs — your sequence phrases are their only map.

Clear time signposts (At first, A few minutes later, Suddenly, By the time, In the end) guide the listener from the opening scene to the turning point, and a final reflection shows why the experience mattered.

Pattern:

Opening & sequence: At first … · A moment later … · After that … · All of a sudden … · Finally …

Tight time links: Earlier that morning … · By the time … · As soon as …

Natural examples:

• At first, everyone at the table stayed quiet. Then, all of a sudden, my grandfather started laughing.

• As soon as I opened the envelope, I knew the hard work had paid off.

• Looking back, that mistake taught me to check the schedule twice.

Keep in mind:

→ 'As soon as' shows that the second action happened immediately after the first, with no gap in between.

Part 3 · See the Difference

Three camera angles in the past: event vs scene vs earlier flashback

Notice how changing the tense in the second clause completely changes the timeline of the meal in these three sentences:

Past simple (next event)

Past continuous (in progress)

Past perfect (already finished)

How the timeline changes

When my sister arrived, I cooked dinner.

When my sister arrived, I was cooking dinner.

When my sister arrived, I had cooked dinner.

1. Past simple: she arrived first, and then I started cooking. 2. Past continuous: I was in the middle of cooking when she walked in. 3. Past perfect: the food was already cooked and waiting on the table before she arrived.

He took a taxi when the rain started.

He was taking a taxi when the rain started.

He had taken a taxi before the rain started.

Each tense places his ride at a different point relative to the rain: after it started, during it, or before it.

The three-part architecture of a memorable spoken story

When you tell an anecdote in conversation or in a speaking exam, give it a clear three-part shape: 1. Set the scene (past continuous: where you were, what was happening). 2. Tell the key events in order, flashing back only when needed (past simple + past perfect). 3. Land the ending with what changed or what you learned (past simple or present perfect): 'It was pouring with rain… I slipped on the steps because I had rushed out in smooth shoes… I've checked the weather before leaving the house ever since.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. While I __________ (study) for the final exam, the electricity suddenly went off.

2. We __________ (already / eat) dinner by the time our cousins arrived.

3. First, I __________ (call) the clinic, and then I __________ (take) a taxi across town.

4. She __________ (walk) along the riverbank when she __________ (see) smoke rising from the warehouse.

5. By 2019, he __________ (finish) his engineering degree and started his first job.

6. The children __________ (play) in the courtyard while their mother __________ (rest) indoors.

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Combine into one sentence using while: 'I read the contract. The office printer jammed.'

2. Combine using by the time and the past perfect: 'We reached the station. The train left.'

3. Correct the timeline mistake: 'When I arrived at the hall, the speaker already left.'

4. Use sequence signposts (At first, Suddenly, In the end) to tell a three-sentence story about nearly missing a bus or flight.

5. Choose the natural connector: The doorbell rang (while / when) I was drying my hair.

6. Rewrite this flat list as a vivid two-sentence story scene using past continuous and past perfect: 'It rained hard. I forgot my umbrella at work. I got soaked.'

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Take turns telling a two-minute true story from your own life. While you listen to your partner, picture the scene and prepare two genuine follow-up questions about details that make you curious.

• Choose one prompt: a journey you still remember clearly · a day when plans went wrong in an unexpected way · an important decision you had to make quickly.

• Include all three story layers: a clear opening scene (past continuous), at least one earlier detail that had happened before the main moment (past perfect), and a closing line that explains why the moment mattered.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: It was a cold Tuesday morning in January, and I was waiting for a shared taxi outside the university. I had stayed up until two in the morning finishing my project, so I was half asleep...

B: Oh no — did you make it to the presentation on time, or had the professor already started when you walked in?

Your conversation goal: Each partner tells a two-minute story that the other can retell in three sentences, and asks two genuine follow-up questions about it.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ opens with a clear background scene using the past continuous

✓ guides the listener with natural sequence signposts

✓ uses the past perfect accurately to mark an earlier action

✓ ends with a clear reflection on why the experience mattered

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

Once your three basic narrative tenses work smoothly together, you can add texture to your storytelling by showing repeated past routines, highlighting how long an earlier activity had been going on, and connecting a past story to who you are today.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Before you start speaking, picture the three layers of your story: what was happening in the background (was/were + -ing), what happened next (past simple), and what had already happened earlier (had + past participle).

• Practise telling a compact 30-second anecdote aloud that includes one 'while', one 'when', and one 'by the time'.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use 'would + base verb' (or 'used to') to paint nostalgia or repeated past habits at the start of a story: 'On summer evenings in my hometown, we would sit in the orchard and listen to my uncle's stories.'

• Use the past perfect continuous (had been + verb-ing) to show how long an activity had been in progress before the turning point: 'We had been waiting in the rain for forty minutes when the bus finally appeared.'

• Close your story by bridging back to the present with the present perfect: 'That afternoon taught me a lesson I've never forgotten.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take ten seconds of silent mental planning (write nothing down): picture your opening background scene, the two main events in order, one earlier detail that explains why it happened (had + participle), and your closing reflection.

Speak without reading: Tell a two-minute story about a memorable day in your life — a small crisis, an unexpected kindness, or a lucky break. After your partner gives feedback, switch partners and tell the same story a second time, making the sequence and ending even sharper.

Model response — speak first, then compare

It was a Friday afternoon in May. I was walking home from the bookshop when I suddenly realised I had left my phone on the counter — I had only been walking for ten minutes, so I turned back at once. At first I checked my coat pockets twice; then I hurried back down the street. By the time I reached the shop, the owner had already answered a call from my cousin: he had won two tickets to the championship final and needed my answer straight away. I called him back from the shop counter, and we went to the stadium that evening. I've checked my pockets before leaving every shop ever since.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ clear three-part story shape (background scene → main events → closing reflection)

✓ natural sequence signposts (at first, then, by the time, in the end)

✓ past continuous and past perfect used accurately to separate time layers

✓ the listener can easily retell the main events in the right order

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Past continuous paints the background scene in progress; past simple moves the main events forward; past perfect flashes back to an earlier past action.

• Sequence signposts (at first, suddenly, by the time, as soon as) keep your listener oriented.

• Strong spoken stories end by showing what changed or what the speaker learned.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'When I arrived, he left.' (means he left after I arrived) → 'When I arrived, he had already left.' (means he was gone before I arrived).

→ 'While I was walking, I had seen an old friend.' → 'While I was walking, I saw an old friend.' (Use past simple, not past perfect, for the main interrupting event.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Tell a 30-second true or invented story aloud that uses both 'while' and 'by the time'.

• Name the three layers of a well-structured story and give one example sentence for each.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ My spoken stories have a clear background scene, logical sequence, and meaningful ending.

☐ I can use the past perfect naturally to show which of two past actions happened first.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 2 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. was studying · 2. had already eaten · 3. called / took · 4. was walking / saw · 5. had finished · 6. were playing / was resting

Practice B: 1. While I was reading the contract, the office printer jammed. · 2. By the time we reached the station, the train had left. · 3. When I arrived at the hall, the speaker had already left. · 4. answers vary · 5. while · 6. It was raining hard, and because I had forgotten my umbrella at work, I got soaked. (answers vary)

LESSON 3 · QUESTIONS, AUXILIARY VERBS, AND FOLLOW-UP QUESTIONS

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: ask clear questions and keep a conversation alive

Why do some English conversations feel effortless while others feel like a stiff border-control interview? Usually it comes down to how people ask questions. When a speaker drops auxiliary verbs, uses direct interrogation word order with strangers, or jumps from one unrelated topic to the next, the conversation stalls.

When you master three habits — clean question word order, polite indirect openings, and follow-up questions that build on what the other person just said — you can keep any conversation alive and make the other person feel genuinely heard.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Compare these two short exchanges:

• Exchange 1: A: 'Where you work?' B: 'At a bank.' A: 'What is your favourite food?'

• Exchange 2: A: 'What kind of work do you do?' B: 'I work at a bank.' A: 'Really? What part of banking do you focus on?'

With a partner, find out three things about each other: their favourite way to unwind after a busy week, something they are trying to learn this year, and one place they hope to visit. Rule for this warm-up: after every answer, you must ask ONE follow-up question about what your partner just said before changing the subject.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Forming direct questions: auxiliaries and the subject-question exception

Most direct English questions put an auxiliary verb (do, does, did, am, is, are, have, has, will, can, should) in front of the subject: 'Where do you live?' or 'Have you finished the report?' Once 'do', 'does', or 'did' carries the tense, the main verb returns to its base form: 'Did she call?' (never 'Did she called?').

There is one crucial exception that trips up even experienced speakers: when the question word itself (Who, What, Which) is the subject of the verb, there is no inversion and no 'do/did'. Compare: 'Who called you?' (Someone called you — 'Who' is the subject) versus 'Who did you call?' (You called someone — 'you' is the subject).

Pattern:

Yes/No question: Auxiliary + subject + main verb …? → Do you agree? · Have they arrived?

Wh- object question: Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + main verb …? → Where did she go?

Subject question (Who/What = subject): Wh- subject + verb …? → Who wrote this? · What happened?

Natural examples:

• Where do you usually study in the evenings?

• Did the coordinator send the new timetable yesterday? (base verb 'send' after 'did')

• What happened at the end of the meeting? ('What' is the subject — no 'did')

• Who organised the workshop, and who did you invite to speak? (subject question vs object question)

Keep in mind:

→ After do, does, or did, always use the base verb: 'Where did you buy that?' (not 'Where did you bought that?').

→ Test whether Who or What is the subject by answering the question in your head: 'Who broke the cup?' → 'Ali broke it' (subject = no 'did').

Rule 2 — Polite indirect questions: softening the approach

Walking up to a professor, a client, or a stranger and asking 'Where is the office?' or 'How much does this cost?' is grammatically correct, but it can sound abrupt. To sound polite and composed, English speakers wrap the question inside a soft opening phrase such as 'Could you tell me…?' or 'Do you know…?'

Here is the golden rule of indirect questions: the opening phrase already does the work of asking the question, so the second half switches back to normal statement word order (subject + verb) and drops 'do/does/did'.

Pattern:

Direct question: Wh- word + auxiliary + subject + verb? → Where is the bank? / When did he leave?

Indirect question: Polite opener + Wh- word (or if/whether) + subject + verb → Could you tell me where the bank is? / Do you know when he left?

Natural examples:

• Could you tell me where the registration desk is?

• Do you happen to know what time the library closes on Fridays?

• I'd like to know when the interview results will be announced.

• I was wondering if you could look over my draft this afternoon.

Keep in mind:

→ Never invert twice! Say 'Do you know where the bank is?' (not 'Do you know where is the bank?').

→ For Yes/No indirect questions, connect with 'if' or 'whether': 'Do you know if the bus has left?'

Rule 3 — Follow-up questions: the engine of real conversation

Good conversationalists do not memorize a list of twenty questions. Instead, they ask one clear opening question, listen for an interesting word or feeling in the answer, and ask a follow-up question about that exact detail.

Content follow-ups show your partner that you are actually listening to their story, not just waiting for your turn to talk.

Pattern:

Quick reactions + follow-ups: Really? What happened next? · How did you decide to do that?

Digging deeper: You mentioned it was challenging — which part was hardest? · What would you do differently next time?

Natural examples:

• A: I switched from engineering to teaching last year. B: That's a big step — what made you decide to change?

• A: I took the speaking test twice before I got the score I needed. B: What did you change between the first attempt and the second?

Keep in mind:

→ Build your follow-up from the content of your partner's sentence rather than switching topics: echo one key idea they mentioned and ask 'Why?', 'How?', or 'What was that like?'

Part 3 · See the Difference

Direct vs polite indirect questions in the same situation

Notice two changes when you move from the direct column to the polite column: the tone becomes much more respectful, and the verb moves back after the subject.

Direct (quick / casual)

Indirect (polite / professional)

What changes in the grammar

Where did you buy that dictionary?

Could you tell me where you bought that dictionary?

After 'Could you tell me where', we drop 'did' and put the past tense back on the verb ('you bought').

What time does the clinic open?

Do you know what time the clinic opens?

After 'Do you know what time', we drop 'does' and use statement order ('the clinic opens').

Why was the flight delayed?

Would you mind telling me why the flight was delayed?

The auxiliary 'was' moves after 'the flight' so the embedded clause reads like a statement.

Subject questions vs object questions — why "Who" works two ways

Compare two questions about the same phone call: suppose Mariam called Tariq.

• If we ask 'Who called Tariq?', the answer is Mariam (the subject). Because 'Who' stands in the subject's shoes, the verb follows directly: 'Who called Tariq?'

• If we ask 'Who did Mariam call?', the answer is Tariq (the object), and Mariam is the subject. Because 'Mariam' is the subject, we need the auxiliary 'did' before her name: 'Who did Mariam call?'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. __________ you ever __________ (try) traditional Kabuli palaw cooked over wood fire?

2. What __________ (happen) at the end of the department meeting yesterday?

3. Do you know where __________ ? (the main library / be)

4. Could you tell me how much this course __________ ? (cost)

5. Who __________ (write) this summary on the board?

6. Who __________ you __________ (speak) to at the admissions office yesterday?

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Make this question polite for a stranger: 'Where did you park your car?'

2. Make this question polite for an administrator: 'When will the exam results be ready?'

3. Correct the word-order mistake: 'Do you know where is the nearest pharmacy?'

4. Write two natural content follow-up questions for a partner who says: 'I'm planning to change careers next year.'

5. Correct the verb mistake: 'Did she called you after the interview?'

6. Write one question starting with 'How long…' to ask a classmate about a skill or hobby they have.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Run a three-minute conversational interview with your partner. Partner A starts by asking about one of the topics below, but every conversation must stay on that single topic for at least three follow-up exchanges before moving on. Then swap roles.

• Choose three topics from: learning English · a moment you felt proud of your work · a difficult decision you had to make · a plan for the next two years.

• Each partner must use at least one polite indirect question ('Could you tell me…', 'I was wondering…') and at least three content-based follow-up questions.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: I was wondering what your biggest goal is for the next year.

B: I'm hoping to apply for a master's programme abroad.

A: Really? Do you know which university you want to apply to, or are you still comparing options?

Your conversation goal: A three-minute exchange per pair in each role: three answers, at least three content-based follow-ups, one indirect question — then a one-sentence summary of what you learned about your partner.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ question word order is accurate in both direct and indirect questions

✓ follow-up questions build directly on details the partner just shared

✓ the conversation flows naturally without abrupt topic jumps

✓ both partners speak and ask questions in balanced measure

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

In real conversation, questions do more than request missing facts — they also express surprise, check shared understanding, and invite agreement.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Contrast direct and embedded order aloud until your ear catches inversion errors automatically: 'Where did you go?' versus 'Do you know where you went?'

• Keep five polite openers ready for formal and professional situations: 'Could you tell me…', 'Do you happen to know…', 'Would you mind telling me…', 'I was wondering if…', 'Do you have any idea…'

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use negative questions to express surprise or polite expectation: 'Haven't we met before?' or 'Didn't you receive the schedule I sent?'

• Use short echo questions when a detail surprises you and you want the speaker to elaborate: 'You waited how many hours at the airport?'

• Use natural question tags with falling intonation to invite agreement and keep the listener engaged: 'It's been a busy week, hasn't it?' · 'You've worked with Dr Rahimi before, haven't you?'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 30 seconds to prepare: write down one single-sentence story opener of your own (for example, 'I almost missed an important flight last year' or 'I tried cooking for twenty guests last month'), plus two polite indirect question frames you can use during the conversation.

Speak without reading: Two-minute conversation challenge: Partner A says only their one-sentence opener. Partner B must keep the conversation going for two full minutes by asking natural follow-up questions, reacting genuinely, and using at least one indirect question — while Partner A answers naturally and asks questions back.

Model response — speak first, then compare

A: I almost missed my flight last week.
B: Really? What happened?
A: The main road to the airport was closed, so I reached the check-in desk twenty minutes before boarding. Do you travel often, or do you prefer staying close to home?
B: I fly for work a few times a year. Could you tell me how you managed to get through security in time?
A: One of the staff saw my boarding pass and took me to the front of the queue. Have you ever missed a connection?
B: Not a flight, but I missed the last bus from Herat once. How did you feel when you finally sat down on the plane?

Partner listening checklist:

✓ asks genuine follow-up questions that react to content rather than switching topics

✓ uses at least one polite indirect question with statement word order

✓ maintains accurate auxiliary and subject-question grammar throughout

✓ keeps the two-minute exchange lively and balanced from start to finish

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Most direct English questions put an auxiliary before the subject — except when Who or What is the subject of the verb ('Who called you?').

• Polite indirect questions ('Could you tell me…', 'Do you know…') switch to statement word order and drop 'do/does/did'.

• Follow-up questions that react to specific details turn a dry Q&A into a real conversation.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'Do you know where is the bank?' → 'Do you know where the bank is?' (Use statement word order inside an indirect question.)

→ 'Did she called you?' → 'Did she call you?' ('Did' already carries the past tense.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Take one question about your city or school and say it twice: first as a direct question, then as a polite indirect question.

• Say one subject question ('Who…') and one object question ('Who did…') using the same verb.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can ask polite indirect questions without accidentally inverting the verb.

☐ I can keep a conversation moving for two minutes using natural follow-up questions.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 3 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. Have / tried · 2. happened · 3. the main library is · 4. costs · 5. wrote · 6. did / speak

Practice B: 1. Could you tell me where you parked your car? · 2. Do you know when the exam results will be ready? / Could you tell me when the exam results will be ready? · 3. Do you know where the nearest pharmacy is? · 4. answers vary (e.g. 'What field are you thinking of moving into?' / 'What made you decide to make a change?') · 5. Did she call you after the interview? · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'How long have you been studying English?')

LESSON 4 · MODAL VERBS FOR REAL-LIFE SITUATIONS

Part 2 — Express Ideas Clearly | Speaking goal: express ability, advice, obligation, permission, possibility and certainty at the right strength

Suppose a colleague shows you a draft of an important email that has several confusing sentences. If you say, 'You must rewrite this,' you sound like a strict commander. If you say, 'You might want to make the second paragraph a little clearer,' you sound like a helpful teammate.

Modal verbs (can, could, should, must, might, would) are the volume controls of English. They let you adjust the exact social strength of your advice, requests, obligations, and logical guesses so your listener hears both your message and your respect.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Imagine two real-life moments with a partner:

• Situation 1: A close friend tells you, 'I study English for two hours every night, but I still freeze when I have to speak.' Give them two pieces of helpful advice.

• Situation 2: You need to leave today's class or work meeting fifteen minutes early for a medical appointment. How would you ask the instructor or manager?

Compare the exact words you both chose. Which words made your advice sound encouraging rather than bossy, and which words made your request sound polite?

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Choosing modals by meaning and social strength

Structurally, core modal verbs are the simplest verbs in English: they are followed directly by the base verb for every person, with no '-s' in the third person and no 'to' ('She can swim', 'He should wait').

The real skill is choosing the right modal for the relationship. 'Must' and 'have to' express necessity or strong obligation; 'should' and 'ought to' offer advice; 'can', 'could', and 'may' handle ability, possibility, and permission.

Pattern:

Modal + base verb (never add -s or 'to': he can speak · she should wait · you mustn't touch)

Obligation: must / have to · Advice: should / ought to · Possibility: may / might / could · Ability & permission: can / could / may

Natural examples:

• All applicants have to submit their transcripts by Friday. (external institutional rule)

• You really must try the fresh bread from that bakery! (speaker's personal enthusiasm / strong recommendation)

• You should take a short break before you drive home. (supportive advice)

• We could meet on Wednesday, or we might wait until the report is ready. (open possibilities)

Keep in mind:

→ 'Have to' usually points to an external rule or situation ('I have to wear an ID badge at work'), whereas 'must' often expresses the speaker's own authority or personal conviction ('I must remember to call my mother tonight').

→ In the negative, their meanings split completely: 'don't have to' means it is not necessary ('You don't have to bring food'), while 'mustn't' means it is forbidden ('You mustn't park in front of the ambulance bay').

Rule 2 — Degrees of certainty: reading the evidence

We also use modal verbs when we look at clues in front of us and make a logical guess (a deduction). Suppose you knock on a colleague's office door and nobody answers.

If her coat is on the chair and her computer screen is on, you say, 'She must be in the building' (you are almost certain it is true). If you have no idea where she is, you say, 'She might / may / could be in a meeting' (it is one possibility). If you just saw her drive out of the car park, you say, 'She can't be in her office' (you are almost certain it is impossible).

Pattern:

Present deduction: must be (almost certainly true) · may / might / could be (possible) · can't be (almost certainly not true)

Past deduction: must have + past participle · may / might / could have + participle · can't / couldn't have + participle

Natural examples:

• He has been travelling for fourteen hours — he must be exhausted.

• Take a warm jacket; the temperature might drop after sunset.

• That can't be Bilal at the door — he's in Kandahar all week.

• She isn't answering her phone; she must have left it in her bag.

Keep in mind:

→ For negative logical deductions, always use 'can't be' (never 'mustn't be'): say 'He can't be at home — all the lights are off' (deduction from evidence), whereas 'He mustn't leave the room' is a prohibition.

Rule 3 — Diplomatic and polite framing in real life

When you ask a favour, make a complaint, or suggest a change at work, stepping back from 'can/will' to softer forms ('could', 'would', 'might') gives the other person room to say yes comfortably.

Pattern:

Polite requests: Could I possibly …? · Would you mind + verb-ing …? · I was wondering if I could …

Diplomatic suggestions: It might be worth + verb-ing … · We could always … · You might want to …

Natural examples:

• Would you mind moving your bag slightly so I can sit down?

• Could I possibly have an extra day to check the figures?

• I was wondering if we could reschedule our meeting for Thursday afternoon.

Keep in mind:

→ Because 'Would you mind…?' literally means 'Would it bother you…?', a polite 'yes, go ahead' answer uses a negative word: 'No, not at all' or 'Of course not — go right ahead.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

must vs have to vs should — choosing the right weight

Hear how the social pressure changes across these three ways of talking about seeing a doctor:

must / mustn't

have to / don't have to

should / shouldn't

What the listener hears

You must see a doctor today.

You have to see a doctor to get a medical certificate.

You should see a doctor if that cough continues.

'Must' carries urgent personal insistence from the speaker; 'have to' states an external requirement; 'should' gives sensible, non-pushy advice.

You mustn't work on Saturday.

You don't have to work on Saturday.

You shouldn't work every Saturday.

'Mustn't' forbids it; 'don't have to' says it is optional; 'shouldn't' advises against it for your well-being.

can't (logical deduction) vs mustn't (prohibition)

This is one of the most important contrasts in spoken English:

• Deduction ('can't'): 'The restaurant can't be open yet — the chairs are still on the tables.' (I am judging from the evidence that it is impossible.)

• Prohibition ('mustn't'): 'You mustn't use your phone in the examination hall.' (It is against the rules.)

can't = logically impossible

mustn't = forbidden by rule

Why the difference matters

He can't be home yet — his car is gone.

He mustn't leave yet — the guests are arriving.

Using 'mustn't' for a guess makes you sound as if you are giving an order rather than drawing a conclusion.

could vs was able to for past achievements

Use 'could' for general past ability ('I could swim when I was six'), and also with verbs of perception ('I could hear the music from outside'). When you talk about managing to succeed in one specific, difficult past situation, use 'was/were able to' (or 'managed to'): 'The road was blocked, but after an hour we were able to find another route' (not 'we could find another route'). In the negative, both forms work everywhere: 'We couldn't / weren't able to find it.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. You look exhausted after that double shift. You __________ get some rest tonight. (supportive advice)

2. My grandmother __________ speak four languages fluently when she was a young teacher. (general past ability)

3. Dr Karimi __________ be in the clinic today — his car is parked right outside the entrance. (strong positive deduction)

4. Visitors __________ touch the laboratory equipment — it is high-voltage and dangerous! (prohibition)

5. Take an umbrella just in case; it __________ rain later this afternoon. (possibility)

6. __________ you mind __________ (open) the window for a few minutes?

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Rewrite this blunt command as a polite request: 'Open the window.'

2. Rewrite using a modal of deduction: 'I am almost certain she is at home right now.'

3. Rewrite using a past modal of possibility: 'Perhaps he missed the early train.'

4. Correct the modal mistake: 'He mustn't be at home — all his lights are off.' (intended meaning: I'm sure he isn't)

5. Write a natural, polite reply agreeing to this request: 'Would you mind waiting five minutes?'

6. Give gentle, diplomatic advice to a classmate who has a bad headache (write two sentences using different modals).

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Work with your partner as two colleagues on an organising committee. Your department has a small budget and one free weekend, and you must agree on ONE shared option from the three choices below.

• Options: (1) a two-day communication workshop, (2) upgrading the student study lounge, or (3) a one-day team excursion outside the city.

• Negotiate naturally using modals at different strengths: make suggestions (should / could), point out rules or budget limits (have to / mustn't), make logical guesses about how people will react (must be / might), and use polite requests (Would you mind… / Could we…).

How it sounds in conversation:

A: I think we should invest in the study lounge — the current chairs must be ten years old, and students use that room every day.

B: That's true, though a communication workshop could help everyone before the exam period. Would you mind if we priced the chairs first to see if we might afford a half-day workshop too?

Your conversation goal: One agreed decision per pair, justified with at least three different modals, plus two polite request forms used naturally during the negotiation.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ chooses modal strength that fits the situation (gentle advice vs firm rule)

✓ uses polite request or suggestion frames at least twice (Would you mind… / Could we…)

✓ uses deduction modals accurately based on evidence (must be / might be / can't be)

✓ reaches a clear joint decision and explains the reasoning

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

To sound truly natural in professional and academic speaking, notice how modals extend into the past and how subtle phrases soften suggestions when speaking to senior colleagues or clients.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Sort modals by the job they do in context rather than on a single mechanical scale: must be = strong logical deduction from evidence; should be = reasonable expectation ('The bus should be here soon'); may / might / could be = open possibilities.

• Look around the classroom or out of the window and make three spoken deductions right now: one with 'must be', one with 'might be', and one with 'can't be'.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use past deduction forms (must have / might have / can't have + past participle) to interpret past events: 'You must have been relieved when you saw your name on the list.'

• Use 'would' to soften preferences and recommendations: 'I'd suggest waiting until Monday' · 'Would you prefer morning or afternoon?'

• Use diplomatic obligation frames when proposing changes to a team: 'We really ought to consider…' · 'It might be worth reviewing the schedule before we commit.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take one minute to choose your role and prepare three keywords: your main problem or goal, two polite modal frames you will use ('I was wondering if…', 'Could we possibly…'), and one deduction you can make about the situation ('There must have been…', 'You must be…'). Swap roles after one minute.

Speak without reading: Role-play a real-world problem call: one partner is a client or student dealing with a problem (a delayed book order, a double-booked room, or a missed registration deadline); the other is the professional resolving it. Explain the issue politely, make deductions, propose options, and agree on a solution. Then switch roles.

Model response — speak first, then compare

Client: Good morning — I was wondering if I could speak to someone about my textbook order. It was due on Tuesday, and it still hasn't arrived.
Professional: I'm very sorry about that. You must be frustrated, especially with classes starting this week. Let me check the tracking number… Ah, it looks as if the parcel was sent to the wrong district depot.
Client: In that case, could I possibly have it delivered tomorrow? I have to teach until four, so it might need to arrive in the evening.
Professional: That should be possible. We could book an evening courier slot for you, or I could have the main bookshop hold a fresh copy for you to collect today. Which would you prefer?

Partner listening checklist:

✓ modals match the intended social strength (polite request, gentle advice, firm obligation)

✓ maintains a composed, polite tone even while explaining a problem

✓ includes at least one natural deduction (must be / must have been / can't be)

✓ arrives at a practical solution that both speakers accept

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Core modals are followed directly by the base verb (no -s, no 'to') and let you adjust the strength of advice, obligation, and possibility.

• Use 'must be', 'might be', and 'can't be' for logical deductions from evidence; never confuse 'can't be' (impossible) with 'mustn't' (forbidden).

• Softening frames ('Could I possibly…', 'Would you mind + -ing…', 'I was wondering if…') keep requests and negotiations polite.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'He mustn't be at home.' → 'He can't be at home.' (Use 'can't' when you mean 'I am sure it isn't true'.)

→ 'Would you mind to open the window?' → 'Would you mind opening the window?' ('Mind' takes the -ing form.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Make three logical deductions about people or things around you using 'must be', 'might be', and 'can't be'.

• Ask a partner for a small favour in two different ways using polite modal openings.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can adjust how strong or polite my advice and requests sound in conversation.

☐ I can make present and past deductions accurately using must, might, and can't.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 4 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Practice B: 1. Could you open the window, please? / Would you mind opening the window? · 2. She must be at home. · 3. He might have missed the early train. / He may / could have missed the early train. · 4. He can't be at home — all his lights are off. · 5. No, not at all. / Of course not — take your time. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'You should drink some water and rest your eyes. You might also want to step outside for some fresh air.')

2. While we __________ (wait — ongoing action), the announcement came.

3. At standard atmospheric pressure, pure water __________ (freeze) at 0°C.

4. She __________ (study) medicine these days.

2. __________ you mind __________ (close) the door?

3. Do you know where the post office __________ ? (be)

4. You __________ bring any food; we will provide everything. (not / have to)

2. Make it polite: 'Where did you park?' (Could you tell me…)

LESSON 5 · CONDITIONALS FOR DECISIONS AND POSSIBILITIES

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: talk about consequences, alternatives and hypothetical situations accurately

Listen to two managers discussing a project delay. The first says, 'If we get the parts tomorrow, we'll finish on Friday.' The second says, 'If we got the parts tomorrow, we'd finish on Friday.' Both sentences talk about tomorrow, yet the first manager expects the parts to arrive, while the second manager doubts they will show up at all.

Conditionals are how English speakers weigh decisions, test possibilities, and learn from past mistakes. By shifting the verb tense in the 'if' clause, you tell your listener immediately whether you are dealing with a real plan, a hypothetical daydream, or a past event that cannot be undone.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Read these three sentences aloud with a partner and notice how your view of the situation changes:

• 'If I have free time this evening, I'll call my brother.'

• 'If I had more free time these days, I'd learn photography.'

• 'If I had known about the traffic this morning, I would have left home half an hour earlier.'

Which sentence talks about a real possibility today? Which one imagines a different present? Which one looks back at a past moment that is already over? Now tell your partner one real plan for this week (using the first pattern) and one change you would make if you had an extra free day every week.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Zero and first conditionals: real facts and real future possibilities

When you talk about the real world — things that always happen or things that can genuinely happen tomorrow — keep the 'if' clause in the present tense.

Use the zero conditional (If + present, present) for scientific truths, rules of nature, and automatic habits. Use the first conditional (If + present, will + base verb) when a future condition is genuinely open and you are predicting or promising the result.

Pattern:

Zero conditional (always true): If / When + present simple, present simple

First conditional (real future possibility): If + present simple, will (or can / may / should) + base verb

Natural examples:

• If you heat ice above 0°C, it melts. (general law of nature)

• If I drink coffee after dinner, I don't sleep well. (personal habit that always holds true)

• If the weather stays clear tomorrow, we'll hike up to the ridge. (real future possibility)

• If you finish the draft by four, I can check it before I leave. (real condition with a modal result)

Keep in mind:

→ In an ordinary future condition, use the present simple in the if-clause: say 'If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay home' (do not use 'will' just because the event is in the future). Will can occur in if-clauses with a special meaning such as polite willingness ('If you will wait a moment, I'll fetch the director'), but ordinary future conditions take the present simple.

Rule 2 — Second conditional: imagining a different present or unlikely future

What if you want to talk about a situation that is not true right now, or a future scenario that you consider unlikely? English steps one tense back into the past simple in the 'if' clause, and uses 'would' (or 'could / might') in the result clause.

The past tense here does not point to yesterday — it signals distance from reality. When you say 'If I had her phone number, I would call her right now,' your listener immediately knows two things: you do not have the number now, and therefore you cannot call.

Pattern:

Second conditional: If + past simple, would / could / might + base verb → unreal present · unlikely future · hypothetical advice

Natural examples:

• If I had an extra hour every morning, I would read in English before work. (reality: I don't have that hour now)

• If I were you, I'd accept the fellowship offer immediately. (hypothetical advice)

• If public transport were faster, fewer commuters would drive into the city centre.

Keep in mind:

→ In advice and careful English, 'If I were you…' (and 'If he/she/it were…') is the conventional standard form. 'Was' also occurs in informal conversation ('If I was you…'), but 'If I were…' works well in every setting.

Rule 3 — Third and mixed conditionals: looking back at the past

The third conditional is our time machine for hindsight. Because the past is already finished, we step one level further back to the past perfect (If + had + past participle) and use 'would have + past participle' for the imagined past result.

Sometimes, however, a past choice still shapes your life right now. When a past event has a present result (or a permanent present trait caused a past action), we mix the two halves into a mixed conditional.

Pattern:

Third conditional (both halves in the past): If + past perfect, would / could / might have + past participle

Mixed (past cause → present result): If + past perfect, would + base verb (now)

Mixed (present trait → past result): If + past simple (always), would have + past participle (then)

Natural examples:

• If we had left ten minutes earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train. (third: we left late, and we missed it)

• If I had accepted that job in Herat, I would live there now. (mixed: past decision → present life)

• If she weren't so organized, the conference wouldn't have run so smoothly last week. (mixed: permanent trait → past result)

Keep in mind:

→ In natural spoken English, both 'had' and 'would' contract to 'd: 'If I'd known you were waiting, I'd have called.' Never put 'would have' inside the if-clause (say 'If I had known', not 'If I would have known').

Rule 4 — Beyond "if": unless, as long as, and provided that

You do not have to begin every condition with 'if'. When you want to set a clear boundary or exception, 'unless' means 'except if / if not', while 'as long as' and 'provided (that)' mean 'on the condition that'.

Pattern:

unless + affirmative verb = if … not · as long as / provided (that) = only if

Natural examples:

• You won't notice progress unless you practise speaking out loud. (= if you don't practise)

• I'm happy to lend you my notes as long as you return them by Thursday.

• Provided that everyone arrives on time, the meeting will finish by eleven.

Keep in mind:

→ Because 'unless' already means 'if not', do not add a second negative inside the unless-clause: say 'Unless you hurry, we'll be late' (not 'Unless you don't hurry').

Part 3 · See the Difference

First vs second vs third conditional — one situation across three worlds

Compare how a speaker uses three different conditionals depending on whether the opportunity is still open, unlikely, or already gone:

Option A

Option B

What changes in the speaker's mind

If I have time this afternoon, I'll help you.

If I had time this afternoon, I would help you.

1st conditional = real possibility (my schedule might allow it). 2nd conditional = unreal present (my afternoon is already full, so I am politely apologizing that I cannot).

If I knew her email, I would write to her.

If I had known her email yesterday, I would have written to her.

2nd conditional = present gap (I don't know it now). 3rd conditional = past hindsight (yesterday's chance has already passed).

Third conditional vs mixed conditional — where does the result live?

When you start a sentence with 'If I had slept earlier last night…', pause for a split second and ask: is the result also in the past, or is it happening right now?

Third conditional (past result)

Mixed conditional (present result)

How to choose

If I had slept earlier last night, I would have caught the eight o'clock bus.

If I had slept earlier last night, I wouldn't feel so tired right now.

Left (3rd): catching the bus was this morning (past). Right (mixed): feeling tired is right now (present).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. If you __________ (heat) pure water at sea level to 100°C, it __________ (boil).

2. If it __________ (rain) heavily tomorrow morning, we __________ (cancel) the outdoor training session.

3. If I __________ (be) in your position, I __________ (apologise) to the client in person.

4. If she __________ (leave) home fifteen minutes earlier, she __________ (not/miss) the train yesterday.

5. If I __________ (know) his new phone number, I __________ (call) him right now.

6. We __________ (go) for a walk along the river as long as the weather __________ (stay) dry.

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Rewrite using unless: 'If you don't register before Friday, you can't attend the seminar.'

2. Rewrite as a third conditional: 'He didn't check the timetable, so he missed the ferry.'

3. Rewrite as a mixed conditional (past cause → present result): 'She didn't save enough money last year, so she can't buy the car now.'

4. Correct the mistake: 'If I will have free time tonight, I will review the vocabulary.'

5. Use a second conditional ('If I were you…') to advise a friend who wants to quit their job tomorrow without another offer.

6. Answer in your own words with a full second conditional sentence: What would you do if you were given a one-year scholarship to study anywhere?

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Play a cause-and-effect chain game with your partner. You will build two short stories together, sentence by sentence, where the result of one speaker's conditional becomes the 'if' clause of the next speaker's sentence.

• Chain 1 (looking back and connecting to now): Start with 'If I had woken up an hour earlier this morning…' Build at least six connected sentences together, including both third and mixed conditionals.

• Chain 2 (imagining a change tomorrow): Start with 'If the internet stopped working across the whole city for a week…' Build six connected sentences exploring what people would do.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: If I had woken up an hour earlier this morning, I would have caught the early bus.

B: And if you had caught the early bus, you wouldn't have run into the morning traffic jam — so you would feel much more relaxed right now!

Your conversation goal: One shared story of at least six linked conditional sentences per pair, including one third and one mixed conditional, that both partners can retell in summary.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ conditional verb forms match the intended time (real future, unreal present, unreal past)

✓ includes at least one third conditional and one mixed conditional accurately

✓ each sentence builds logically on the partner's previous idea

✓ both partners contribute equally without reading from notes

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

In formal presentations, debates, and storytelling, English speakers often vary their conditional openings so they do not repeat the word 'if' in every sentence.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Keep one clear anchor sentence in mind for each conditional pattern: 'If you heat ice, it melts' (zero) · 'If it rains, we'll cancel' (first) · 'If I were you, I'd wait' (second) · 'If I'd known, I'd have come' (third).

• Practise saying the natural spoken contractions aloud ('If I'd known…', 'We'd have waited…', 'She wouldn't have minded') so three-part verbs roll off your tongue smoothly.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use inverted conditionals in formal talks by dropping 'if' and placing Should, Were, or Had at the start: 'Should you require any further details, please let us know' · 'Had we known about the shortage, we would have ordered earlier.'

• Use 'but for + noun phrase' as a compact alternative to a negative conditional clause: 'But for your timely advice, we would have signed the wrong contract.'

• Use 'suppose' or 'supposing (that)' when inviting a listener to explore a scenario with you: 'Suppose our budget were cut by twenty percent — which project would we protect first?'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 30 seconds to assign each conditional a clear job for your talk: a first conditional for the realistic outcome of your choice, a second conditional for an option you are rejecting, and a third or mixed conditional for a lesson learned from last year. Jot down only three or four keywords.

Speak without reading: One-minute decision talk: Imagine your school or workplace has received a special grant. You must choose ONE of three investments: (1) staff training, (2) new computer equipment, or (3) a student resource library. Explain what will happen if you choose your top option, why the second option is less effective, and what you would have done differently with last year's budget.

Model response — speak first, then compare

If we invest this grant in staff training, our whole team will improve their teaching skills, and students will feel the benefit within a month. Buying new computers would look impressive at first, but if I were leading the committee, I would put people ahead of hardware every time. In fact, if we had set aside a small training fund last year, we wouldn't be facing such a steep learning curve with the new curriculum right now. Provided that we schedule the workshops before the new term starts, training is by far the smartest choice.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ uses a first conditional for realistic future consequences

✓ uses a second conditional to weigh a hypothetical alternative or give advice

✓ uses a third or mixed conditional to reflect on a past decision

✓ connects the options into a persuasive, logical recommendation

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Zero conditional states general truths; first conditional predicts real future possibilities (using the present simple after 'if').

• Second conditional ('If + past, would + verb') imagines an unreal present or unlikely future; 'If I were you…' is the classic advice frame.

• Third conditional ('If + had + participle, would have + participle') looks back at an unchangeable past; mixed conditionals connect a past cause to a present result.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'If it will rain tomorrow, we'll stay in.' → 'If it rains tomorrow, we'll stay in.' (Use present simple for ordinary future conditions.)

→ 'Unless you don't hurry, you'll miss the bus.' → 'Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.' ('Unless' already means 'if not'.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Say one sentence of your own for each conditional type: zero, first, second, third, and mixed.

• Take one real mistake or delay from your past month and turn it into a third conditional sentence.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can distinguish smoothly between an unreal present (second conditional) and an unreal past (third conditional).

☐ I can link a past decision to a present result using a mixed conditional.
