Practice A: 1. heat / boils · 2. rains / will cancel (or: 'll cancel) · 3. were / would apologise · 4. had left / wouldn't have missed · 5. knew / would call · 6. will go / stays

Practice B: 1. Unless you register before Friday, you can't attend the seminar. · 2. If he had checked the timetable, he wouldn't have missed the ferry. · 3. If she had saved enough money last year, she could buy the car now. / …would be able to buy the car now. · 4. If I have free time tonight, I will review the vocabulary. · 5. answers vary (e.g. 'If I were you, I wouldn't resign until I had a signed offer in hand.') · 6. answers vary

LESSON 6 · WISHES, REGRETS, AND HYPOTHETICAL SITUATIONS

Part 3 — Think Beyond the Present | Speaking goal: express preferences, dissatisfaction, regrets and imagined alternatives naturally

When you hope something will happen tomorrow, you stay in the real world: 'I hope the bus comes soon.' When you wish something were different right now, you already know reality is the opposite: 'I wish I had an umbrella with me' (said while standing in the rain with no umbrella).

Because wishes, regrets, and polite preferences often describe a world that does not match reality, English uses the same clever device you saw in conditionals: stepping one tense back in time to signal that you are imagining an alternative.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Compare these three sentences spoken by a student on the morning of an exam:

• 'I wish I knew the answer to question four.' (during the exam)

• 'I wish I had studied chapter seven last night.' (looking back at yesterday evening)

• 'I wish the person behind me would stop tapping their pen.' (reacting to an annoying noise)

With a partner, discuss how the speaker feels in each sentence and what time each sentence points to. Then share one skill you wish you had right now and one small decision from the past year you would handle differently.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Wishing for a different present: wish + past simple, could, or would

When you want your current reality to be different right now, follow 'wish' (or the more emphatic 'If only') with the past simple: 'I wish I spoke Arabic fluently' means 'I do not speak it fluently right now.'

When the wish is about your own ability, use 'could' ('I wish I could stay longer'). When you want someone else — or an outside situation — to change their behaviour, use 'would' ('I wish you would listen before interrupting').

Pattern:

Present state wish: wish / if only + past simple → I wish I knew her address. (reality: I don't know it)

Present ability wish: wish / if only + could + base verb → I wish I could join you.

Desired change in behaviour/situation: wish / if only + somebody/something + would + base verb

Natural examples:

• I wish our flat were closer to the university. (were is the traditional subjunctive and common in careful English; was is also widespread informally: I wish our flat was closer.)

• I wish I could remember where I put that folder.

• I wish the neighbours wouldn't play loud music after midnight.

Keep in mind:

→ Use 'wish + would' when you want someone else's behaviour or an outside situation to change (it often carries a note of impatience or complaint). We do not say 'I wish I would…' about ourselves — for our own ability, use 'I wish I could…'.

Rule 2 — Wishing for a different past: regrets with wish + past perfect

When a moment is already in the past and you regret what happened (or didn't happen), step one level further back to the past perfect: 'wish + had + past participle'.

'If only…!' uses the exact same grammar as 'I wish…', but adds stronger personal emotion.

Pattern:

Past regret: wish / if only + had (not) + past participle → I wish I had started earlier.

Natural examples:

• I wish I had asked more questions during the training week.

• She wishes she hadn't spoken so sharply during the argument.

• If only we had checked the road conditions before setting off!

Keep in mind:

→ Never use 'wish + past simple' for a finished past event: for yesterday's mistake, say 'I wish I hadn't said that yesterday' (not 'I wish I didn't say that yesterday').

Rule 3 — Expressing preferences and overdue actions: would rather and it's time

'Would rather' changes its grammar depending on who is doing the action. When you talk about your own preference, use the base verb: 'I'd rather walk than wait for the bus.' When you want someone else to do something, introduce a new subject and step back to the past simple: 'I'd rather you didn't mention this to anyone yet.'

Similarly, 'It's time' (or 'It's high time') followed by a subject and a past simple verb means an action is already overdue — it should have happened before now: 'It's ten o'clock — it's time we headed home.'

Pattern:

Same subject (my own action): would rather (not) + base verb (than …) → I'd rather stay in tonight.

Different subject (someone else's action): would rather + person + past simple → I'd rather you called me tomorrow.

Overdue action: It is (high / about) time + subject + past simple → It's high time we made a decision.

Natural examples:

• I'd rather cook a simple meal at home than wait an hour at a crowded restaurant.

• I'd rather you didn't park in front of the gate — the delivery lorry needs to get through.

• It's high time the city council repaired this bridge.

Keep in mind:

→ Do not confuse 'would rather' (preference) with 'had better + base verb' (strong urgent warning: 'You'd better leave now or you'll miss your flight').

Rule 4 — Comparing preferences and describing impressions: prefer and as if / as though

With 'prefer', watch how you connect the two options: 'prefer A to B' (with nouns or -ing forms) versus 'would prefer to do A rather than do B'.

With 'as if' and 'as though', use the past simple or past perfect when the comparison is unreal or exaggerated: 'He gives orders as if he owned the company' (he does not own it).

Pattern:

General preference: prefer + noun/-ing + to + noun/-ing · Specific choice: would prefer + to + verb + rather than + base verb

Unreal impression: act / look / talk + as if / as though + past simple (present unreal) or past perfect (past unreal)

Natural examples:

• I generally prefer reading printed books to reading on a screen.

• Today I'd prefer to walk rather than take a taxi.

• She walked back into the meeting room calmly, as though nothing had happened.

Keep in mind:

→ If what follows 'as if' is a real, likely fact based on evidence, keep the normal present tense: 'Look at those dark clouds — it looks as if it is going to pour.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

Present wish vs past regret — stepping back in time

Notice how the verb form after 'wish' tells the listener immediately whether the situation can still be changed today or belongs to the past:

wish + past simple (present reality)

wish + past perfect (past regret)

What the listener understands

I wish I had a quieter room to study in.

I wish I had chosen a quieter room when we moved in.

Left (past simple): my room is noisy right now. Right (past perfect): I am looking back with regret at the past choice I made.

I wish I knew how to fix this engine.

I wish I had learned how to fix engines at college.

Left: I am stuck in front of the engine right now. Right: I regret missing the opportunity years ago.

wish + could vs wish + would — ability vs willingness

wish + could (personal ability)

wish + would (other person's choice)

Why the choice matters

I wish I could come to your graduation.

I wish you would come to my graduation.

'Could' points to inability (I have an exam that day, so I am unable to attend). 'Would' appeals to the other person's willingness (you are free, and I want you to decide to come).

Three ways to use 'It's time' — from neutral to urgent

Compare the tone of these three sentences:

1. 'It's time to leave.' (neutral statement — the scheduled moment has arrived).

2. 'It's time we left.' (gently insistent — we are already a little late).

3. 'It's high time he took responsibility for his work.' (emphatic criticism — this is long overdue).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. I wish I __________ (know) her email address so I could send her the invitation right now.

2. I really wish I __________ (not/say) that careless remark during yesterday's meeting.

3. He gives everyone instructions as if he __________ (own) the entire department.

4. It's high time we __________ (make) a firm decision about the autumn budget.

5. I'd rather you __________ (not/tell) anyone about the job offer until the contract is signed.

6. If only I __________ (be) a little more patient when traffic slows down!

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Rewrite as a past regret using wish: 'I didn't study harder at school, and now I regret it.'

2. Rewrite politely using would rather: 'Please don't smoke near the doorway.'

3. Correct the tense mistake: 'I wish I have more free time this semester.'

4. Correct the tense mistake: 'It's already midnight — it's time we will go home.'

5. Choose the natural forms: I generally prefer (reading / to read) historical novels to (watch / watching) television.

6. Write one vivid sentence with 'as if' or 'as though' describing a friend who arrived late and out of breath.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Play 'The Constructive Adviser' with your partner. Partner A shares three honest frustrations or regrets from everyday life using 'I wish…', 'If only…', or 'I'd rather…'. Partner B listens, asks one clarifying question, and offers a practical step forward using 'It's time…', 'You could…', or 'If I were you…'. Swap roles after two minutes.

• Choose three areas from: study habits · work-life balance · health and sleep · learning English · technology use.

• Include at least one present wish (wish + past simple/could/would), one past regret (wish + past perfect), and one response with 'It's time we/you…' or 'I'd rather…'.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: I wish I didn't spend so much time checking my phone late at night — I always wake up tired.

B: I know that feeling. It's about time we both left our phones in another room after ten o'clock. If you bought a simple alarm clock, you wouldn't need your phone beside your bed at all.

Your conversation goal: Three complaint–solution exchanges per role: each complaint uses a correct wish form, each solution a natural modal or 'it's time', and partners swap roles smoothly.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ distinguishes accurately between present wishes (wish + past) and past regrets (wish + past perfect)

✓ uses 'It's time + past simple', 'would rather', and advice modals naturally

✓ reacts thoughtfully to the partner's situation rather than reading a list

✓ both partners complete all three exchanges in each role

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

Notice how skilled speakers use these same hypothetical patterns to soften workplace requests, add emotional colour to stories, and express diplomatic dissatisfaction.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Separate your own real-life wishes into two clear mental buckets: what you wish were different today ('I wish I knew / had / could…') versus what you wish had happened differently in the past ('I wish I had known / done…').

• Say three true sentences aloud right now: one with 'I wish I knew…', one with 'I wish I had known…', and one with 'I'd rather you…'.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use 'If only…!' when you want to convey stronger personal feeling or dramatic emphasis in a story: 'If only we had backed up the files before the power cut!'

• Use past-continuous framing ('We were hoping…', 'I was wondering…') to express diplomatic wishes in professional settings: 'We were hoping the figures would be ready before Friday.'

• Use 'as though' with the past perfect to describe revealing body language in a narrative: 'He greeted everyone cheerfully, as though the argument the night before had never happened.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 30 seconds to note three keywords: one genuine past regret that taught you something useful (wish + past perfect), one present habit or skill you still wish to change (wish + past simple / could), and one practical piece of advice for someone younger.

Speak without reading: Speak for one full minute: 'A mistake or regret that taught me an important lesson.' Describe what you wish you had done differently in the past, what you still wish you could do better today, and what advice you would give a younger student facing the same choice.

Model response — speak first, then compare

I wish I had taken spoken English seriously during my first two years at university — I wasted countless classes staying silent because I was afraid of making small grammar slips. Even today, I sometimes wish I could express complex technical ideas as effortlessly as my mentor does. But that regret taught me something valuable: fluency only grows when you use the language out loud. It's high time we stopped treating mistakes as failures. If I were advising a first-year student today, I'd tell them to record themselves speaking for two minutes every week — within a month, you can hear the difference.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ uses 'wish + past perfect' (or 'If only + past perfect') accurately for the past regret

✓ uses 'wish + past simple' or 'wish + could' for the present situation

✓ turns the regret into constructive advice using a conditional, modal, or 'It's time…'

✓ speaks naturally and reflectively without reading from notes

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Use 'wish + past simple / could' for present situations you want to be different; use 'wish + past perfect' for regrets about a finished past.

• Use 'wish + person/thing + would' when you want someone else's behaviour or an external situation to change.

• When 'would rather' or 'It's (high) time' is followed by a subject, step back to the past simple ('I'd rather you waited' · 'It's time we left').

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'I wish I have more time.' → 'I wish I had more time.' (Present wishes step back to the past form.)

→ 'I'd rather you don't mention this.' → 'I'd rather you didn't mention this.' (Use past simple after a new subject.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Say one honest present wish and one honest past regret from your own life.

• State one preference about your own evening ('I'd rather…') and one polite preference about someone else's action ('I'd rather you…').

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can express both present wishes and past regrets without mixing up their verb tenses.

☐ I can use 'would rather', 'It's high time', and 'as if' naturally in conversation.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 6 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. knew · 2. hadn't said · 3. owned · 4. made · 5. didn't tell · 6. were (or: was in informal speech)

Practice B: 1. I wish I had studied harder at school. · 2. I'd rather you didn't smoke near the doorway. · 3. I wish I had more free time this semester. · 4. It's already midnight — it's time we went home. · 5. reading / watching · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'He burst through the door out of breath, as if he had run all the way from the station.')

LESSON 7 · COMPARISONS BEYOND THE BASICS

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: compare clearly and support comparisons with reasons

When someone says, 'Option A is better than Option B,' they have stated an opinion, but they have not yet persuaded anyone. Compare that with: 'Option A is far more reliable than Option B because it costs half as much to maintain, and the longer we use it, the more money we save.'

Every real-world recommendation — choosing a university course, hiring a candidate, defending a budget — is built on comparison. When you combine accurate comparative forms with precise degree words and clear reasons, your opinions turn into persuasive arguments.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Read these two pairs of claims aloud with a partner:

• 'Train travel is better than flying.' vs. 'On short routes, train travel is far more relaxing than flying because you avoid airport security queues.'

• 'Vocabulary is important.' vs. 'The more actively you use new vocabulary in speech, the faster it becomes permanent.'

Now take one minute each to compare two ways of learning (studying alone vs studying in a group, or learning online vs in a classroom). Give at least one specific reason for your choice.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Comparatives and superlatives: comparing choices vs identifying an extreme

Comparatives compare two people, things, or sets ('shorter than', 'more practical than'), while superlatives single out an extreme within a group ('the shortest', 'the most practical'). Use a comparative to compare two people, things or sets. Use a superlative to identify an extreme within a group, which often contains three or more. The exact number is a guide, not a grammatical rule: context and meaning decide.

Short one-syllable adjectives (and many two-syllable adjectives ending in -y, like easy → easier) take '-er' and 'the -est'. Longer adjectives of two or more syllables take 'more' and 'the most' (or 'less' and 'the least').

Pattern:

Short adjectives: adj-er + than · the + adj-est (fast → faster → the fastest · busy → busier → the busiest)

Longer adjectives & adverbs: more/less + adj/adv + than · the most/least + adj/adv

Irregular forms: good/well → better → the best · bad/badly → worse → the worst · far → further/farther → the furthest/farthest

Natural examples:

• Taking the ring road is quicker than driving through the old bazaar.

• She explained the financial plan more clearly than the previous consultant.

• That was the most challenging — and the most rewarding — project of my career.

Keep in mind:

→ Never stack 'more' and '-er' together: say 'much taller' or 'far better' (never 'more taller' or 'more better').

→ Spell and pronounce the comparison link as 'than' (not 'then', which refers to time).

Rule 2 — Equality, multiples, and linked change: as … as and the more …, the more …

Not every comparison says one thing is bigger or better than another. Sometimes you want to show that two options are equal ('as effective as'), that one falls short ('not as expensive as'), or that one is a specific multiple of the other ('twice as fast as').

When two changes move together in cause and effect, English uses the double-comparative frame 'The + comparative …, the + comparative …': 'The more you speak out loud, the more natural the grammar feels.'

Pattern:

Equality & gap: (not) as + adjective/adverb + as · twice / three times / half + as + adj/adv + as

Linked change: The + comparative …, the + comparative …

Continuous trend: comparative + and + comparative (faster and faster · more and more competitive)

Natural examples:

• This compact dictionary is just as comprehensive as the heavy two-volume edition.

• Practising aloud for twenty minutes is twice as effective as rereading notes silently for an hour.

• The earlier we leave tomorrow morning, the less traffic we will face on the highway.

• Solar panels are becoming more and more affordable every year.

Keep in mind:

→ Inside 'as … as', keep the adjective or adverb in its base form: 'twice as expensive as' (not 'twice more expensive than').

→ In 'the more …, the more …', both halves must use a comparative form: 'The harder you prepare, the calmer you feel.'

Rule 3 — Calibrating your comparison: degree words that persuade

Saying 'Course A is better than Course B' leaves your listener wondering: is it 2% better or 200% better? Adding a precise modifier in front of your comparative or superlative ('far more practical', 'slightly more expensive', 'by far the best') shows that you have weighed the evidence carefully.

Pattern:

Large difference: far / much / a great deal / значительно → significantly + comparative

Small difference: slightly / a little / marginally + comparative · almost / nearly as … as

Emphatic superlative: by far + the + superlative · easily + the + superlative

Natural examples:

• The evening train is slightly slower than the express bus, but it is far more comfortable.

• This year's results were not nearly as predictable as last year's.

• Deliberate speaking practice is by far the most effective way to build fluency.

Keep in mind:

→ Always compare like with like: compare one city's climate with another city's climate ('The winter here is milder than in Bamyan' or 'than Bamyan's winter'), and back up every major comparison with 'because…'.

Part 3 · See the Difference

Comparative vs superlative — weighing two options vs crowning a standout

Comparative (weighing choices)

Superlative (extreme in a group)

How the meaning shifts

This textbook is clearer than the one we used last term.

This is the clearest textbook in the department library.

Comparatives weigh options against each other; superlatives identify an extreme within a whole group or category.

The northern route isfar safer than the mountain pass in winter.

The northern route is by far the safest option in winter.

'Far' intensifies a comparative ('far safer'); 'by far' intensifies a superlative ('by far the safest').

Small modifiers that flip the meaning of "as … as"

Expression A

Expression B

What your listener hears

The second exam was just as difficult as the first.

The second exam was not nearly as difficult as the first.

'Just as' means 100% equal in difficulty; 'not nearly as' means the second exam was much easier.

The sooner we start, the better.

Sooner or later, we will have to start.

'The sooner, the better' links speed to a better result; 'sooner or later' simply means 'eventually'.

Turning a flat opinion into a persuasive comparison

Whenever you compare two ideas in a speaking test or meeting, use this three-step formula: 1. Degree modifier + comparative ('Studying in short daily sessions is far more effective than weekend cramming…') 2. Concrete reason ('…because your brain consolidates memory between sessions…') 3. Linked outcome ('…and the more consistently you review, the less you forget under exam pressure.')

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. Taking the side street is __________ (short) than waiting at the main roundabout.

2. Waiting six hours at a freezing bus station was __________ (bad) travel experience of my life.

3. The __________ (much) you read in English, the __________ (fast) your vocabulary grows.

4. She presented the team's findings __________ (confidently) than anyone expected.

5. Repairing the old generator is not __________ expensive __________ buying a brand-new one.

6. He is by far the __________ (talented) debater in our graduating class.

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Rewrite using twice as … as: 'The new battery lasts two times longer than the old one.'

2. Correct the mistake: 'My younger brother is more taller than me now.'

3. Strengthen this comparison with 'far' and add a 'because' reason: 'Practising with a partner is better than studying alone.'

4. Build a 'The more …, the more …' sentence of your own about building confidence in speaking.

5. Correct the spelling/usage mistake: 'This dictionary is much clearer then my old one.'

6. Compare three cities or towns you know: use a comparative to contrast two of them, and a superlative to name which one you would most like to live in and why.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Play 'The Persuasive Recommender'. Each partner has 30 seconds to recommend one choice in the same category (for example, the best time of day to study, the best way to travel across the country, or the most useful skill for a young graduate). Then debate your choices politely and agree on one joint recommendation.

• In your recommendation, include at least: one comparative with a degree word (far, much, slightly), one superlative (or 'by far the…'), and one 'as … as' or 'the more …, the more …' sentence.

• Every comparison must be supported by a concrete reason ('because…'). Finish by agreeing on one winner together.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: Studying early in the morning is far more productive than studying late at night because your mind is fresh and the house is quiet.

B: Morning study is quieter, that's true, but for me evening study is just as effective as long as I turn off my phone. Still, I agree that the earlier you finish your hardest task, the better the rest of your day feels.

Your conversation goal: Two 30-second recommendations, each containing at least three accurate comparisons with reasons, followed by one agreed joint choice stated aloud.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ comparative and superlative forms are accurate (no double comparatives)

✓ every comparison is backed up by a clear reason

✓ uses at least two degree modifiers (far, much, slightly, by far, not nearly)

✓ reaches and states a polite joint recommendation at the end

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

In academic discussions and professional presentations, speakers rarely make one-sided comparisons; instead, they acknowledge what the other option does well before showing why their choice is stronger.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Master the irregular trios aloud until they are automatic: good / better / the best · bad / worse / the worst · far / further / the furthest.

• Practise pairing degree modifiers with real items in front of you: 'slightly heavier than', 'far more durable than', 'not nearly as complicated as'.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use emphatic superlative frames for confident evaluation: 'by far the most practical solution' · 'the single most important factor' · 'the least likely outcome'.

• Use concessive comparisons to sound fair and persuasive: 'While Option A is slightly cheaper upfront, Option B is far better value in the long run.'

• Use 'Compared with…' or 'In contrast to…' at the start of a sentence to frame evidence cleanly: 'Compared with five years ago, access to online courses has grown dramatically.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 30 seconds to pick one topic below and jot down three comparison keywords: one 'far / much + comparative', one 'by far + superlative', and one 'the more …, the more …' or 'twice as … as' pattern, plus one brief reason for each.

Speak without reading: One-minute persuasion talk: Argue for your view on ONE of these questions — (1) What is the best age to start learning a second language? (2) What is the most effective way to prepare for a high-stakes speaking test? or (3) What is the smartest investment of one free hour every day?

Model response — speak first, then compare

In my view, early childhood is the easiest age to pick up natural pronunciation, because young children imitate sounds far more effortlessly than adults and are much less afraid of making mistakes. However, when it comes to using one hour a day as an adult learner, deliberate speaking practice is by far the most valuable investment you can make. Speaking aloud with a partner is twice as effective as silent review because you get immediate feedback when a sentence is unclear. Compared with memorizing word lists alone, real conversation builds habits that last — and the more regularly you speak, the more natural your grammar becomes.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ accurate comparative, superlative, and equality forms throughout

✓ every comparison is supported by a clear reason or example

✓ uses degree words naturally to calibrate strength (far, much, twice as, by far)

✓ closes with a memorable conclusion that answers the prompt directly

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Comparatives compare two choices; superlatives identify an extreme within a group; 'as … as' expresses equality or multiples ('twice as fast as').

• 'The + comparative …, the + comparative …' links two changing processes together.

• Degree modifiers ('far', 'much', 'slightly', 'by far') and 'because' reasons turn flat opinions into persuasive arguments.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'She is more taller than me.' → 'She is taller than me.' (Never use 'more' with an -er comparative.)

→ 'This route is faster then the highway.' → 'This route is faster than the highway.' ('Than' compares; 'then' marks time.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Make one comparison using 'far more … than' and one sentence using 'The more …, the more …'.

• Name three skills or subjects you have studied, rank them using superlatives, and give one reason for your top choice.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can use comparatives, superlatives, and 'as … as' patterns accurately with degree modifiers.

☐ I can support my spoken comparisons with clear reasons and 'the more …, the more …' sentences.

Practice A: 1. shorter · 2. the worst · 3. more / faster · 4. more confidently · 5. as / as · 6. most talented

Practice B: 1. The new battery lasts twice as long as the old one. · 2. My younger brother is taller than me now. · 3. Practising with a partner is far better than studying alone because you have to respond in real time. (answers vary) · 4. answers vary (e.g. 'The more often you speak in class, the more confident you feel.') · 5. This dictionary is much clearer than my old one. · 6. answers vary

LESSON 8 · LINKING IDEAS AND BUILDING ARGUMENTS

Part 4 — Compare and Persuade | Speaking goal: organise opinions into coherent, well-linked spoken arguments

Have you ever listened to a speaker who had intelligent ideas, yet after thirty seconds you lost track of what they were trying to prove? Usually the problem is not their vocabulary — it is that their sentences arrive with no turn-signals.

Linking words (although, despite, because of, therefore, for instance, to sum up) are the turn-signals of spoken English. They warn your listener in advance whether your next thought is a reason, a concrete example, a concession to the other side, or your final conclusion.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Listen to the difference between these two ways of expressing the same view:

• Speaker A: 'Online courses are popular. Some students drop out. They miss classroom discussion. Online courses save travel time. I think blended learning is best.'

• Speaker B: 'Although online courses save valuable travel time, many students drop out because they miss live classroom discussion. Therefore, I believe a blended approach works best.'

Read both versions aloud with a partner. Then speak for 30 seconds each on 'Why people in our city learn English' while your partner counts how many different linking expressions you use naturally.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Contrast and concession: although vs despite vs however

When you want to show an unexpected contrast between two facts, English gives you three tools — and each tool requires a different grammatical package after it.

Use 'although' or 'even though' before a full clause (subject + verb). Use 'despite' or 'in spite of' before a noun phrase or an -ing verb form (never a bare subject + verb). Use 'however', 'nevertheless', or 'on the other hand' to open a brand-new sentence (or clause after a semicolon), followed by a comma.

Pattern:

Clause linker: Although / Even though + subject + verb, main clause

Noun / -ing linker: Despite / In spite of + noun phrase or verb-ing, main clause

Sentence connector: First sentence. However, / Nevertheless, / On the other hand, second sentence.

Natural examples:

• Although the snow was heavy, the morning bus arrived on schedule. (subject 'the snow' + verb 'was')

• Despite the heavy snow, the morning bus arrived on schedule. (noun phrase 'the heavy snow')

• Despite waking up with a migraine, she delivered her presentation clearly. (-ing form)

• The proposal involves some initial risk. Nevertheless, the committee voted to approve it.

Keep in mind:

→ Never mix 'despite' and 'in spite of' into 'despite of' — say either 'despite the delay' or 'in spite of the delay'.

→ If you want to put a subject + verb after 'despite', insert 'the fact that': 'Despite the fact that it was snowing, we went out.'

Rule 2 — Cause, result, and purpose: matching the grammar to the linker

Just like contrast linkers, cause linkers divide into a clause family and a noun family. Use 'because', 'since', or 'as' before a full clause (subject + verb); use 'because of', 'due to', or 'owing to' before a noun phrase.

To introduce a logical consequence, use 'therefore', 'as a result', or 'consequently'. To express the purpose of an action, use 'in order to / to + base verb' or 'so that + subject + modal verb'.

Pattern:

Cause (+ clause): because / since / as + subject + verb · Cause (+ noun): because of / due to + noun phrase

Result: therefore / as a result / consequently · Purpose: in order to + verb · so that + subject + can/could/will/would

Natural examples:

• We postponed the match because the pitch was flooded. (+ full clause)

• We postponed the match because of / due to the flooded pitch. (+ noun phrase)

• Public libraries extended their evening hours; as a result, student attendance doubled.

• I recorded the lecture so that my classmate could listen to it while recovering at home.

Keep in mind:

→ Keep 'because' and 'therefore' in separate jobs: 'because' introduces the reason, while 'therefore' introduces the result. Do not use both to join the same two clauses.

Rule 3 — Building an argument you can deliver out loud

When you are asked for your opinion in a meeting, interview, or speaking exam, do not just state what you think and stop. Give your listener a clear four-step architecture: state your Point, explain your Reason, make it concrete with an Example, and close with a short Link or Summary.

Three well-connected sentences with a real example are far more persuasive than ten disconnected claims.

Pattern:

1. POINT: I firmly believe that … / In my view, … → 2. REASON: This is mainly because …

3. EXAMPLE: For instance, … / To give a concrete example, … → 4. ADDITION: Moreover, … / What is more, …

Natural examples:

• In my view, every university course should include short weekly presentations. This is mainly because graduates need to explain their ideas clearly at work. For instance, in my cousin's engineering firm, junior staff present project updates every Monday. Moreover, regular practice removes the fear of speaking in public.

Keep in mind:

→ Acknowledge the other side briefly before stating your main point ('Although exams test individual memory, presentations prepare students for real teamwork') — a speaker who addresses counterarguments sounds fair and authoritative.

Rule 4 — Ordering points and landing a memorable summary

When your listener cannot see your notes, verbal signposts ('First of all…', 'Another key factor is…', 'To sum up…') act like headings for the ear and make your conclusion stick.

Pattern:

Sequencing points: First of all, … · Secondly, … · Another key point is that …

Closing summary: To sum up, … · All in all, … · In short, …

Natural examples:

• To sum up, the long-term benefits of staff training clearly outweigh the initial cost.

• All in all, I would recommend starting with a two-week pilot programme.

Keep in mind:

→ Listeners remember the last sentence you say best — always finish an opinion talk with a crisp summary line.

Part 3 · See the Difference

One contrast, three grammatical packages: although vs despite vs however

See how the exact same idea changes its grammatical shape depending on which linker you choose:

although + clause

despite + noun / -ing

however + new clause

How the grammar works

Although the traffic was heavy, we arrived on time.

Despite the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.

The traffic was heavy; however, we arrived on time.

'Although' takes a subject + verb ('the traffic was'); 'Despite' takes a noun phrase ('the heavy traffic'); 'However' opens the second independent clause.

because (+ clause) vs because of (+ noun)

because + subject + verb

because of + noun phrase

What changes

Because she worked tirelessly, the clinic succeeded.

Because of her tireless work, the clinic succeeded.

Adding 'of' turns 'because' into a prepositional phrase, so it must be followed by a noun phrase ('her tireless work') rather than a verb.

Direct contrast (while / whereas) vs concession (although)

Use 'while' or 'whereas' when you are simply placing two different facts side by side on a scale: 'My brother enjoys bustling city life, whereas I prefer quiet mountain towns.'

Use 'although' or 'even though' when the first fact makes the second fact surprising: 'Although I usually prefer quiet mountain towns, I really enjoyed my year working in the capital.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. __________ the heavy morning traffic, everyone arrived at the examination centre on time. (Despite / Although)

2. __________ feeling exhausted after the night shift, she stayed to brief the morning nurse. (Despite / Although)

3. He failed his first driving test; __________, he practised every afternoon and passed the next month. (however / despite)

4. We left home at six in the morning __________ we could cross the pass before midday. (so that / because of)

5. The main highway was closed by snow. __________, all flights out of the valley were fully booked. (As a result / Although)

6. I prefer working in a quiet library, __________ my study partner learns best by discussing ideas aloud. (whereas / despite)

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Combine into one sentence using although: 'The assignment was challenging. Every group finished on time.'

2. Combine into one sentence using despite + -ing (or a noun phrase): 'She was not selected the first time. She applied again the following year.'

3. Correct the mistake: 'Despite of the high cost, the hospital purchased the new scanner.'

4. Build a three-sentence spoken argument (Point → Reason → Example) supporting the statement: 'Reading widely improves spoken English.'

5. Correct the mistake in two different ways: 'Although the rain, the football match continued.'

6. State two brief advantages of technology in education, then close with a summary sentence starting with 'To sum up,' or 'All in all,'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Hold a polite two-minute mini-debate with your partner on the motion below. First, Partner A argues in favour and Partner B argues against; after two minutes, switch sides and argue the opposite position so you practise seeing both sides of an issue.

• Debate motion: 'Written homework in language classes should be replaced by daily recorded speaking practice.'

• In each turn, follow the argument skeleton (Point → Reason → Example), acknowledge one point from your partner's side using 'Although…' or 'Despite…', and close with a clear summary sentence.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: I believe daily speaking recordings are far more useful than traditional worksheets. This is because learners need active retrieval under real-time pressure. For instance, when I started recording a two-minute voice note every evening, I noticed my hesitation dropping within two weeks.

B: Although voice recordings build fluency, written homework is still essential because it gives learners time to notice spelling and complex sentence structure...

Your conversation goal: One two-minute mini-debate per role: a clear point with reason and example, one answer to the other side, and a closing summary — followed by a one-sentence verdict you both accept.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ uses contrast and concession linkers accurately (especially despite + noun/-ing vs although + clause)

✓ follows a clear Point → Reason → Example structure

✓ acknowledges and responds to the partner's counterargument

✓ lands a clear closing summary before agreeing on a balanced verdict

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

Strong speakers do not use more linking words — they use the exact right linker to show how two ideas relate, and they use concessive balance to win over skeptical listeners.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Group your linkers by their job in conversation: contrast (although, despite, however, whereas) · cause (because, since, due to) · result (therefore, as a result) · example and summary (for instance, to sum up).

• Practise expressing the same real-life contrast in both grammatical shapes aloud: 'Although the course was demanding…' and 'Despite the demanding course…'.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use 'Not only … but also …' (with inversion when placed at the start of a formal sentence) to build momentum: 'Not only did the programme reduce costs, but it also improved staff morale.'

• Use two-step concessive frames to sound fair and measured in debates: 'It is certainly true that…; nevertheless, …' or 'Admittedly, the initial cost is high; even so, the long-term savings are substantial.'

• Use ', which…' at the end of a clause to comment on the whole consequence of an event: 'The director answered every question openly, which immediately put the staff at ease.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 45 seconds to write down four keywords only: your main claim, two reasons (with one real personal example in mind), and one concession to another viewpoint. Choose your four linkers before you start speaking (for example: because · for instance · although / despite · to sum up).

Speak without reading: Ninety-second opinion talk: 'What makes a truly effective teacher or mentor?' State your main claim, support it with two reasons and a concrete example from your own experience, acknowledge one competing view, and finish with a memorable summary — without looking at notes.

Model response — speak first, then compare

I believe what makes a truly effective teacher is clear, honest feedback combined with patience. This is because learners improve fastest when they know exactly what to adjust without feeling discouraged. For instance, my first English instructor corrected our pronunciation habits every day with a warm smile, and as a result our whole class gained confidence within a month. Although entertaining games can make a classroom lively, I would trade entertainment for clear guidance any day. To sum up, a great teacher shows you the next step clearly and makes you believe you can take it.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ clear Point → Reason → Example → Summary architecture throughout the talk

✓ accurate use of contrast/concession linkers (although + clause or despite + noun/-ing)

✓ natural cause and result connections (because, as a result, therefore)

✓ a crisp closing summary that leaves a clear final impression

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Use 'although / even though' before a full clause (subject + verb); use 'despite / in spite of' before a noun phrase or -ing form; use 'however' to open a new sentence.

• Use 'because' before a clause and 'because of / due to' before a noun phrase; use 'therefore / as a result' for consequences.

• Build spoken arguments on a four-part skeleton: Point → Reason → Example → Summary.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'Despite of the delay, we arrived.' → 'Despite the delay…' or 'In spite of the delay…' (Never say 'despite of'.)

→ 'Although the high price, we bought it.' → 'Despite the high price, we bought it' or 'Although the price was high, we bought it.'

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Deliver a 20-second argument on any everyday topic using 'because', 'for instance', and 'to sum up'.

• Express the same contrast idea in three ways aloud: once with 'although', once with 'despite', and once with 'however'.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can switch smoothly between clause linkers (although, because) and noun/-ing linkers (despite, because of).

☐ I can organize an unscripted 90-second opinion into a clear Point → Reason → Example → Summary structure.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 8 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. Despite · 2. Despite (followed by -ing; 'Although' needs a subject + verb: 'Although she felt exhausted') · 3. however · 4. so that · 5. As a result · 6. whereas

Practice B: 1. Although the assignment was challenging, every group finished on time. · 2. Despite not being selected the first time, she applied again the following year. / Despite the initial rejection, she applied again. · 3. Despite the high cost, the hospital purchased the new scanner. · 4. answers vary — must include a clear point, a reason, and an example · 5. Despite the rain, the football match continued. / Although it was raining, the football match continued. · 6. answers vary — must close with To sum up / All in all / In conclusion

REVIEW TEST 2

Cumulative review — Lessons 1–8 · 15 questions · suggested time: 20 minutes

Part A — Complete the sentences.

1. If I __________ (know) his number, I would call him now.

2. I wish I __________ (take) that opportunity last year.

3. This method is __________ (effective) than the old one.

4. While I __________ (read — ongoing action), the lights went out.

5. When we arrived, the guests __________ (already / leave).

6. It's high time we __________ (make) a decision.

7. This option is by far the __________ (good) for our budget.

8. Unless you __________ (hurry), you'll miss the bus.

Part B — Rewrite, combine or transform.

1. Combine with despite: 'The exam was hard. Everyone passed.'

2. Rewrite as a second conditional: 'I don't have a car, so I can't drive you.'

3. Give polite advice to a friend who wants to quit their job without a plan. (2 modals)

4. Make it polite: 'Where is the bank?'

Part C — Use and communication.

1. Rewrite as a mixed conditional (past → present): 'She didn't save money, so she can't buy the car now.'

2. Compare with a reason: 'This course is better than that one.' (use far + reason)

3. Correct: 'Despite of the cost, we decided to proceed.'
