Quick answers

Practice A: 1. was working · 2. had already submitted · 3. had parked (or: parked) · 4. not to · 5. to help · 6. taking

Practice B: 1. He said (that) he never drank coffee after six in the evening. / He said (that) he never drinks coffee after six in the evening. · 2. They asked when the scholarship results would be announced. · 3. He told me that the train had been cancelled. / He said that the train had been cancelled. · 4. My colleague suggested applying for the fellowship. / My colleague suggested that I apply for the fellowship. · 5. He denied sharing the password with anyone. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'My teacher advised me to read aloud every morning, and my mother reminded me not to skip breakfast before an exam.')

LESSON 14 · PARTICIPLES AND ADVANCED SENTENCE PATTERNS

Part 7 — Sound More Natural and Advanced | Speaking goal: combine ideas concisely without losing clarity

Read this sentence carefully and picture what it literally says: 'Walking down the mountain road, the snowstorm started.' Grammatically, that sentence claims that the snowstorm had two legs and was walking down the mountain road! What the speaker meant, of course, was: 'Walking down the mountain road, we were caught in a snowstorm.'

Participles (-ing and past participles) allow you to compress two bulky clauses into one sleek, authoritative sentence — as long as you keep the subject clear and choose the right participle for the job.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Try combining each pair of sentences below into one smooth sentence aloud with your partner:

• Pair 1: 'She finished the presentation. Then she opened the floor to questions.'

• Pair 2: 'The lecture lasted three hours without a break. The students felt exhausted.'

Now compare: why do we call the lecture 'exhausting' (-ing) but the students 'exhausted' (-ed)? Discuss one experience you found 'exciting' or 'challenging' recently and how you felt during it.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Participle adjectives: -ing (the cause) vs -ed (the feeling)

Many everyday adjectives are built from verbs: boring / bored, confusing / confused, fascinating / fascinated, exhausting / exhausted. Confusing the two endings can lead to unintentional comedy: saying 'I am boring in class' tells your classmates that *you* put *them* to sleep!

Hold on to one simple principle: the '-ing' adjective describes the source that *causes* the feeling, while the '-ed' adjective describes how a person *feels* inside as a result.

Pattern:

Present participle adjective (-ing) → the source / cause of the experience: a confusing instruction · an inspiring talk

Past participle adjective (-ed) → the person experiencing the feeling: confused applicants · inspired listeners

Natural examples:

• The documentary about deep-sea exploration was fascinating, and the audience was fascinated.

• Working a twelve-hour shift at the hospital is exhausting, so the nurses are exhausted by evening.

• The new bus timetable is confusing — even regular commuters look confused.

Keep in mind:

→ A person can be described with '-ing' only when they are the cause of the feeling in others: 'Our history professor is very interesting' (she fascinates her students) versus 'Our history professor is very interested in ancient coins' (she feels curiosity).

Rule 2 — Participle clauses: compressing time, reason, and passive background

Instead of starting every sentence with a heavy clause ('Because she wanted to save time…', 'After he had reviewed the data…', 'The report, which was written in haste…'), you can compress the first clause into a participle phrase — provided both halves of the sentence share the exact same subject.

Use 'Verb-ing…' for an action happening at the same time or as the reason; use 'Having + past participle…' when the first action was clearly completed before the second; and use a 'Past participle…' when the opening idea is passive.

Pattern:

Simultaneous action or reason (active): Verb-ing …, subject + main verb → Walking into the hall, she spotted her friend.

Earlier completed action (active): Having + past participle …, subject + main verb → Having finished the exam, he breathed a sigh of relief.

Passive condition or reason: Past participle (or Having been + participle) …, subject + main verb → Built in 1920, the bridge still carries heavy traffic.

Natural examples:

• Realising that the train was about to leave, we ran to the platform. (= Because we realised…)

• Having lived in Kandahar for ten years, he knew every street in the old city. (= Because he had lived…)

• Warned about the approaching storm, the mountain guides postponed the climb. (= Because they had been warned…)

Keep in mind:

→ In a reduced opening clause with no stated subject, the understood subject should match the main clause: 'Walking to the station, I got soaked' (I was walking), not 'Walking to the station, the rain started.' An absolute clause names its own subject: 'With prices rising, families are worried.'

Rule 3 — Framing a whole situation: Given, Considering, and With + noun + participle

What if you want to set the stage with an outside factor that has its own subject (such as rising prices or an approaching deadline), or frame a professional judgment? English uses two clean patterns that never dangle:

1. Prepositional participle frames ('Given the tight budget…', 'Considering the weather…', 'All things considered…') which are established discourse markers that do not need to match the main subject.

2. Absolute clauses with 'With + noun + participle' ('With the exams approaching, the library is packed'), which explicitly state their own noun subject right after 'With'.

Pattern:

Evaluative frames: Given + noun phrase, … · Considering + noun phrase / that-clause, … · All things considered, …

With-absolute clause: With + noun + verb-ing / past participle, main clause

Natural examples:

• Given the limited rehearsal time, the students delivered an impressive performance.

• With winter approaching rapidly, the municipality repaired the heating pipes.

• Considering how little funding the project received, the results were remarkable.

• All things considered, moving the workshop to Saturday was the right call.

Keep in mind:

→ 'Given' and 'Considering' are exceptionally useful at the start of formal speaking responses because they let you weigh the context before stating your conclusion.

Rule 4 — Keeping compression natural in spoken English

Concision is not about sounding like a legal contract; it is about removing clutter so your key verbs stand out. In spoken English, using one or two well-placed participle openings in a two-minute talk makes you sound composed and articulate — using ten in a row makes you sound unnatural.

Pattern:

Two clauses with the same subject → Participle opening + main clause

Negative participle opening: Not knowing / Not having received …, subject + main verb

Natural examples:

• Not wanting to wake the children, we spoke in whispers.

• Not having received the agenda in advance, several members asked for extra time to read it.

Keep in mind:

→ To make any participle clause negative, place 'Not' (or 'Never') right at the front: 'Not knowing the route, I asked a taxi driver.'

Part 3 · See the Difference

-ing (the source) vs -ed (the experiencer)

-ing adjective (causes the feeling)

-ed adjective (feels the effect)

How to choose instantly

an inspiring speech

an inspired audience

The speech generates the inspiration (-ing); the audience feels it inside (-ed).

frustrating delays

frustrated passengers

The delays cause the frustration (-ing); the passengers experience it (-ed).

Full adverbial clause vs compressed participle clause

Full clause (everyday conversation)

Participle clause (crisp / formal)

What changes

After she had reviewed the patients' charts, she began her rounds.

Having reviewed the patients' charts, she began her rounds.

Both sentences mean the exact same thing; 'Having reviewed…' removes three unstressed words and sharpens the rhythm.

Because the manual was written in clear English, it was easy to follow.

Written in clear English, the manual was easy to follow.

The passive participle 'Written…' attaches directly to 'the manual'.

The subject-matching check — catching dangling participles

In a reduced participle clause with no stated subject, the understood subject should normally match the main clause: 'Opening the door, I felt the cold air' (I opened the door, and I felt the air) — not 'Opening the door, the room was cold' (which makes it sound as if the room opened the door!). Absolute clauses state their own subject, as in 'Weather permitting, we will leave at dawn' or 'With the rain pouring down, we stayed indoors.'

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. The three-hour lecture was so __________ (bore) that several people in the back row nodded off.

2. We were genuinely __________ (amaze) by how quickly the volunteers rebuilt the footbridge.

3. __________ (finish) her keynote speech, Dr Sadat invited questions from the audience. (earlier completed action)

4. __________ (warn) about the icy mountain pass, the drivers fitted snow chains before dawn. (passive participle)

5. __________ fuel prices rising this winter, many commuters are sharing rides to work. (With / Despite)

6. __________ (walk) into the laboratory, she immediately noticed the unlocked cabinet.

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Compress into one sentence using Having + past participle: 'Because she had practised her talk five times, she spoke without hesitation.'

2. Compress by reducing the relative clause: 'The technician who was standing by the generator switched off the power.'

3. Repair the dangling participle so the subject matches: 'Opening the window, the fresh morning breeze cooled the room.'

4. Rewrite more concisely starting with Given: 'When you take the tight deadline into account, the team's report is very thorough.'

5. Correct the adjective mistake: 'I have always been very interesting in architectural history.'

6. Write one sentence of your own starting with 'Having + past participle…' about something you did earlier today.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Play 'The Sixty-Second Executive Briefing'. Take turns giving a calm, concise 60-second briefing to your partner on a recent project, trip, or community event — using participle structures to pack background and reasons cleanly.

• In your 60-second briefing, include: (1) one 'Having + past participle' clause for an earlier step, (2) one framing opener with 'Given…', 'Considering…', or 'With + noun + -ing', and (3) one pair of -ing and -ed adjectives.

• While you listen to your partner, check that every participle opening matches the subject that follows it, then summarize their briefing back in one sentence.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: Given the short notice we received last Monday, our student book fair went remarkably well. Having collected over three hundred donated books during the week, we set up four stalls in the courtyard. The morning setup was exhausting, but everyone felt energised when the first visitors arrived.

B: So having gathered the books in just a few days, you managed to run a busy fair despite the exhausting start!

Your conversation goal: One 60-second briefing per partner containing the three required structures, plus a listener's one-sentence report-back that matches the briefing's content.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ every reduced participle clause matches the subject of the main clause

✓ uses 'Having + past participle' and passive/active participles accurately

✓ distinguishes clearly between -ing (cause) and -ed (feeling) adjectives

✓ maintains natural spoken clarity without overloading a single sentence

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

Used thoughtfully, participle and absolute phrases give formal talks, policy recommendations, and academic summaries a composed, effortless flow.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Test every -ing/-ed adjective pair on real situations from your week: tiring / tired, encouraging / encouraged, overwhelming / overwhelmed, satisfying / satisfied.

• Whenever you start a sentence with an -ing or -ed phrase, make sure the very next word after the comma is the person or thing doing (or receiving) that action.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use negative participle openings for concise reasons: 'Never having spoken in front of a camera before, he practised with a timer first' · 'Not wanting to delay the team, she sent the summary ahead.'

• Use formal absolute expressions when closing a meeting or summarizing a situation: 'Weather permitting, fieldwork will begin on Monday' · 'There being no further objections, the schedule was approved.'

• Close formal recommendations with 'Considering all the evidence,…' or 'All things considered,…' to signal a balanced final judgment.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 45 seconds to choose one practical improvement for your school, university, or workplace (such as shifting morning hours, creating a quiet study zone, or introducing a mentorship system). Jot down three keywords only: the problem evidence ('Given…' or 'Having reviewed…'), your specific recommendation, and your closing judgment ('All things considered…').

Speak without reading: Ninety-second policy recommendation: Present one practical change to improve your school or workplace. Open with 'Given…' or 'Considering…', include at least one 'Having + past participle' clause and one -ing/-ed adjective contrast, and close with 'All things considered…'. Speak without reading.

Model response — speak first, then compare

Given the number of late arrivals during the winter months, I would recommend shifting our first morning seminar from eight o'clock to eight-thirty. Having reviewed the attendance logs from last January, our committee noticed that almost all delays occurred before eight-fifteen, when icy roads make the morning commute frustrating for drivers and passengers alike. Many tired students walk in ten minutes late, missing the opening explanation of the lecture. With classes starting just thirty minutes later, everyone could travel more safely and arrive focused. All things considered, a one-month winter trial costs nothing and would benefit the entire department.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ includes at least two accurate participle or framing structures ('Given…', 'Having reviewed…', 'With…')

✓ keeps the subject of every reduced participle clause aligned with the main clause

✓ uses -ing and -ed adjectives accurately ('frustrating commute', 'tired students')

✓ delivers a clear, composed, and persuasive recommendation

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Use '-ing' adjectives for the source that causes a feeling ('a tiring journey') and '-ed' adjectives for the person who feels it ('tired travellers').

• Participle clauses ('Walking…', 'Having finished…', 'Written in…') compress two clauses into one — make sure their understood subject matches the main-clause subject.

• Use 'Given…', 'Considering…', and 'With + noun + participle' to frame evidence and background formally.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'Opening the window, the room felt cold.' → 'Opening the window, I felt the cold air.' (The room did not open the window!)

→ 'I am very interesting in history.' → 'I am very interested in history.' (People feel '-ed' about a subject.)

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Say one sentence about your morning starting with 'Having + past participle…'.

• Describe a recent class, book, or journey using one '-ing' adjective and one '-ed' adjective.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can compress two connected clauses into a clean participle sentence without losing the subject.

☐ I can use 'Given…', 'Considering…', and -ing/-ed adjectives naturally in formal speech.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 14 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. boring · 2. amazed · 3. Having finished · 4. Warned / Having been warned · 5. With · 6. Walking

Practice B: 1. Having practised her talk five times, she spoke without hesitation. · 2. The technician standing by the generator switched off the power. · 3. Opening the window, I felt the fresh morning breeze cool the room. / When I opened the window, the fresh morning breeze cooled the room. · 4. Given the tight deadline, the team's report is very thorough. · 5. I have always been very interested in architectural history. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Having had a cup of green tea, I sat down to read Lesson 14.')

LESSON 15 · HEDGING, EMPHASIS, AND NATURAL INVERSION

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: control certainty, emphasis and formality like an educated speaker

Imagine two economists on a panel discussion. The first says, 'This tax policy will destroy small businesses.' The second says, 'The evidence suggests that this policy may well place extra pressure on small businesses — and it is the rural shopkeepers who will feel that pressure first.' Who sounds more credible?

Experienced speakers know two secrets of authority: they soften unproved claims so no one can accuse them of exaggerating (*hedging*), and they save their strongest grammatical spotlights (*cleft sentences* and *inversion*) for the one key sentence they want the audience to remember.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Read these two pairs of sentences aloud with a partner, paying attention to tone and voice stress:

• Pair 1 (Certainty): 'Working from home makes people lazier.' vs. 'Working from home can sometimes make it harder to separate rest from work.'

• Pair 2 (Spotlight): 'The practical examples helped me most.' vs. 'What helped me most were the practical examples.'

With your partner, take one controversial opinion about education or work and say it twice: first as a blunt 100% generalisation, and second as a careful, measured claim that an expert would respect.

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — Hedging: matching the strength of your claim to the evidence

In real life, very few social or economic statements are true 100% of the time for 100% of people. When you say 'Social media ruins concentration,' a listener only has to think of one exception to reject your argument.

Hedging is the art of calibrating your claim with modal expressions ('may well', 'could'), tendency verbs ('tend to', 'seem to', 'appear to'), frequency qualifiers ('in many cases', 'broadly speaking'), or impersonal frames ('the data suggests that…', 'it could be argued that…'). Hedging can make a claim sound measured when evidence is limited or a conclusion is uncertain. Academic and professional speakers often hedge; too much hedging, however, can make a message unclear.

Pattern:

Modal hedges: may / might / could + base verb · may well (= quite likely) · is likely to + verb

Tendency verbs: tend(s) to + base verb · seem(s) / appear(s) to + base verb

Evidence & argument frames: The evidence suggests that … · It could be argued that … · In most cases, …

Natural examples:

• Students who study in short daily sessions tend to retain vocabulary longer.

• Upgrading the regional roads may well reduce transport costs by twenty percent.

• The preliminary figures suggest that enrolment has risen this autumn.

• It could be argued that practical apprenticeships are just as valuable as university degrees.

Keep in mind:

→ Use one well-chosen hedge per claim, not three piled on top of each other: 'This policy may well reduce costs' sounds thoughtful; 'Perhaps this policy might possibly seem to reduce costs' sounds unsure.

Rule 2 — Spotlight emphasis: cleft sentences and emphatic "do"

In writing, you can underline or bold a word to make it stand out. In speaking, English gives you a structural spotlight called a *cleft sentence*, which splits a single sentence into two halves so the listener's ear lands squarely on the key point.

Use an 'It-cleft' ('It was the cost that delayed us') to contrast one specific person, thing, or time with others; use a 'Wh-cleft' ('What we need now is clear communication') to build anticipation before delivering your main point; or add 'do / does / did' before a base verb for warm personal emphasis.

Pattern:

It-cleft: It is / was + focused item + that / who + rest of clause → It was Mariam who solved the problem.

Wh-cleft: What + clause + is / was + focused item (or base/to-verb) → What matters most is consistency.

Auxiliary emphasis: Subject + do / does / did + base verb → I do appreciate your patience.

Natural examples:

• It wasn't the grammar rules that held me back — it was my fear of speaking aloud.

• What surprised the researchers most was how rapidly the village adopted solar power.

• We didn't win the tournament, but we did learn how to play as a real team.

Keep in mind:

→ When you speak an It-cleft or auxiliary emphasis sentence, match the grammar with vocal stress on the spotlighted word: 'It was the DEADLINE that forced our hand' · 'She DID call you yesterday.'

Rule 3 — Negative and limiting inversion: formal rhetorical power

When you place a strong negative or limiting expression ('Never', 'Rarely', 'Seldom', 'Not only', 'Only after…', 'Under no circumstances') at the very beginning of a sentence for dramatic or formal emphasis, English flips the subject and auxiliary verb into question word order.

Because inversion is a high-impact rhetorical device, treat it like a trumpet note in a speech: using it once at a key moment commands attention; using it in every paragraph sounds theatrical.

Pattern:

Negative adverbial + auxiliary + subject + verb: Never have I seen … · Rarely does a team achieve … · Seldom had we faced …

Correlative addition: Not only + did/has/is + subject + verb …, (but) … also …

Limiting 'Only' phrase: Only then / Only after + phrase/clause + did + subject + base verb

Natural examples:

• Never have I heard a more practical explanation of the issue.

• Not only did the clinic treat patients free of charge, but it also trained local nurses.

• Rarely do we get a second chance to make a first impression.

• Only after reading the contract a second time did I notice the hidden fee.

Keep in mind:

→ With 'Only after…', 'Only when…', and 'Not until…', wait until the main clause to invert the verb: 'Only when the plane landed did I relax' (do not invert 'the plane landed').

Rule 4 — Calibrating certainty and register to your audience

Notice how English organises probability and formality by meaning and context rather than on a rigid mathematical ladder. When your evidence is solid, state it firmly ('will', 'must be'); when it is probable, signal expectation ('should', 'is likely to', 'may well'); when it is one open possibility among others, keep the door open ('may', 'might', 'could').

Pattern:

Strong prediction / inference: will · must be · Expectation / high likelihood: should · be likely to · may well · Open possibility: may · might · could

Adjusting register: Formal (inversion, clefts, passives, full forms) ↔ Everyday conversation (contractions, direct active verbs)

Natural examples:

• Formal presentation: 'Not only does this approach reduce waste, but it may well lower operating costs.'

• Everyday workplace chat: 'This approach cuts waste, and it'll probably save us money too.'

Keep in mind:

→ A thoughtful hedge signals intellectual honesty — showing your listener that you are matching the strength of your claim to the strength of your evidence.

Part 3 · See the Difference

Three levels of commitment to the same prediction

Firm prediction (will)

Strong likelihood (may well)

Open possibility (could / might)

What your audience hears

The new rail link will transform regional trade.

The new rail link may well transform regional trade.

The new rail link could transform regional trade.

1. 'Will' = firm conviction. 2. 'May well' = strong likelihood based on current signs. 3. 'Could' = one realistic possibility if conditions go well.

Standard word order vs formal negative inversion

Everyday word order

Inverted emphasis (formal)

When to use it

I have never witnessed such determination.

Never have I witnessed such determination.

Same factual meaning, different impact: placing 'Never' first and inverting 'have I' elevates the sentence for a speech or key conclusion.

I understood the problem only after I visited the site.

Only after I visited the site did I understand the problem.

The 'Only after…' opening builds suspense and lands the insight ('did I understand') with sharp focus.

Moving the spotlight with cleft sentences

Direct statement

It-cleft (initial spotlight)

Wh-cleft (end spotlight)

How the focus shifts

The training budget needs urgent attention.

It is the training budget that needs urgent attention.

What needs urgent attention is the training budget.

1. Neutral statement. 2. It-cleft (contrasts the training budget with other budgets). 3. Wh-cleft (builds anticipation before naming the budget at the end).

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. __________ have I heard such a clear and fair summary of the debate. (Never / Ever)

2. Not only __________ (she / pass) the fellowship exam, but she also achieved the highest score in the province.

3. Only after reading the instructions twice __________ (I / understand) how the device worked.

4. The survey data __________ (suggest) that evening classes are popular with working parents. (hedged claim)

5. It was __________ that convinced the committee to approve the project. (spotlight 'the detailed budget')

6. Learners who practise out loud __________ (tend) to build fluency faster than those who only read silently.

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Hedge this sweeping claim so it sounds measured and credible: 'Online learning will replace classrooms everywhere.'

2. Rewrite as an It-cleft focusing on 'the practical examples': 'The practical examples made the lesson easy to follow.'

3. Rewrite using formal negative inversion starting with Rarely: 'We had rarely seen such rapid progress in a single term.'

4. Correct the word-order mistake: 'Never I have seen such a busy market.'

5. Make the same request ('I need two more days to finish the report') at two register levels: (1) to a close teammate, and (2) in a formal meeting with a senior director.

6. Write one sentence about two strengths of a person you admire starting with 'Not only + auxiliary + subject…'.

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Hold a two-person 'Future of Work and Study Panel'. Take turns answering the panel question below for one minute each, using careful hedging for predictions and at least one emphatic structure (a cleft sentence or negative inversion) for your central thesis. Then ask your partner one challenging follow-up question.

• Panel question: 'How will artificial intelligence and online tools change the way people learn and work over the next ten years?'

• In your one-minute view, include: (1) at least two hedged claims ('may well', 'tend to', 'the evidence suggests'), (2) one Wh-cleft or It-cleft ('What will matter most is…' / 'It is… that…'), and (3) one emphatic 'do/did' or inversion.

How it sounds in conversation:

A: While software tools will handle routine translation, it is human judgment and empathy that will become even more valuable. Digital platforms may well make self-study faster, yet rarely do people master persuasive communication without live human feedback.

B: That's a thoughtful point — do you think rural schools will benefit equally from those tools, or could the gap widen at first?

Your conversation goal: Two one-minute answers per partner, each containing one well-placed hedge, one accurate emphasis structure and a clear conclusion — plus one careful answer to the partner's hard follow-up question.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ hedges predictions thoughtfully without stacking too many hedges together

✓ uses at least one cleft sentence or negative inversion accurately

✓ matches the strength of claims to realistic evidence

✓ handles the partner's challenging follow-up question with composure

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

Knowing when to soften a claim and when to spotlight a conclusion is what separates mechanical correctness from genuine rhetorical authority.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Practise expressing the same observation at three levels of certainty in context: firm inference ('will / must be'), reasonable expectation ('should / may well / is likely to'), and open possibility ('may / might / could') — and state what evidence supports each level.

• Say three core inversion frames aloud until the auxiliary-before-subject rhythm feels natural: 'Never have I…' · 'Not only did…' · 'Only then did I…'.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Use 'Little did I know / realise…' to add suspense at a turning point in a spoken story: 'Little did we realise how much that five-minute conversation would change our plans.'

• Use deliberate understatement (litotes) for composed, diplomatic evaluation: 'Reaching agreement across four departments was no small achievement' · 'The initial results are not unpromising.'

• Combine a formal inverted conditional with a hedged result in policy talks: 'Were the municipality to expand the bus network, peak-hour congestion might well fall by a third.'

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take 30 seconds to prepare a two-minute formal talk on improving education or professional training in your country. Jot down three single keywords only: one realistic benefit to hedge ('may well' / 'tends to'), one core priority to spotlight with a cleft ('It is… that…' or 'What we need most is…'), and one strong observation to frame with an inversion ('Rarely…' or 'Not only…').

Speak without reading: Two-minute keynote talk: 'One practical change that would strengthen education in my country.' Include at least one hedged claim, one cleft sentence, and one negative inversion, and finish with a clear, memorable call to action. Speak without reading from notes.

Model response — speak first, then compare

If we want to strengthen education across our country over the next decade, we must look first at practical access. It is reliable internet connectivity in district schools that will determine who benefits from modern learning tools. Rarely have we seen technology advance as rapidly in our major cities as it has in recent years, yet students in smaller towns often study without updated textbooks or digital libraries. Providing solar-powered digital libraries in district centres may well be the most cost-effective educational investment of the decade. Studies suggest that when teachers can share resources easily, classroom engagement rises within a single term. What our students need most is not a more complicated syllabus, but equal access to the tools that already exist.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ uses hedging naturally to make predictions and claims sound credible

✓ uses at least one cleft sentence ('It is… that…' / 'What… is…') to spotlight the central priority

✓ uses one negative or limiting inversion accurately for rhetorical impact

✓ delivers a composed, persuasive two-minute talk with a strong closing line

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• Hedging ('may well', 'tend to', 'the evidence suggests', 'it could be argued') calibrates your claims to your evidence and builds credibility.

• Cleft sentences ('It was X that…', 'What matters most is…') and auxiliary 'do/did' act as vocal spotlights for key information.

• Negative or limiting openers ('Never', 'Rarely', 'Not only', 'Only after…') trigger auxiliary + subject inversion — use them sparingly for high impact.

Common traps to avoid:

→ 'Never I have seen such a crowd.' → 'Never have I seen such a crowd.' (Invert the auxiliary before the subject after a negative opener.)

→ Avoid stacking hedges ('It might possibly perhaps tend to…') or inverting every sentence — clarity and balance always come first.

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Take one prediction about your field of work or study and say it at three levels of certainty: 'will', 'may well', and 'might'.

• Say one 'What… is…' cleft sentence and one 'Not only did…' sentence from memory.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can soften sweeping claims using natural hedging expressions when the evidence is not absolute.

☐ I can spotlight my most important point using a cleft sentence or a well-placed inversion.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 15 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. Never · 2. did she pass · 3. did I understand · 4. suggests (or: suggest) · 5. the detailed budget · 6. tend

Practice B: 1. Online learning may well replace some traditional lectures, or tends to complement classroom study. (answers vary) · 2. It was the practical examples that made the lesson easy to follow. · 3. Rarely had we seen such rapid progress in a single term. · 4. Never have I seen such a busy market. · 5. answers vary (e.g. Teammate: 'Could I have two more days on the report?' / Director: 'I was wondering if it might be possible to extend the deadline by two days so we can verify the final figures.') · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Not only does my mentor listen patiently, but she also gives practical advice.')

LESSON 16 · GRAMMAR IN REAL CONVERSATION

Part 8 — Speak with Confidence | Speaking goal: bring all the course grammar together in free, accurate, confident speech

When a skilled musician walks onto the stage, they are no longer thinking about individual finger exercises — they are listening to the music and shaping the phrase. Speaking a language works the same way. Over the past fifteen lessons, you have built every core grammatical tool you need for real-world English.

This final lesson is not about learning a brand-new rule. It is about seeing how all sixteen lessons fit together on one simple mental map, and mastering the habit that keeps confident speakers moving smoothly even when they slip: natural self-repair.

Part 1 · The Speaking Hook

Start the conversation

Play a 60-second warm-up round with your partner:

• Partner A speaks for 45 seconds without stopping on 'One decision that taught me something important.'

• Partner B listens not only to the story, but also to the grammar tools Partner A uses naturally (tenses, conditionals, linkers, relative clauses, modals, or passives), and names at least three of them at the end. Then swap roles!

Part 2 · The Simple Rule

Rule 1 — The whole course on one mental map: four jobs of spoken grammar

Whenever you open your mouth to answer a complex question — in a university seminar, a job interview, a workplace meeting, or the TOEFL speaking test — you do not need to search through sixteen separate chapters in your head. Every grammar pattern in this book performs one of just four practical jobs:

1. TIME (Lessons 1, 2, 13): placing events in the present, past, future, or reported speech.

2. CHOICE & POSSIBILITY (Lessons 4, 5, 6, 11): expressing modals, conditionals, wishes, and verb patterns (-ing / to).

3. SENTENCE SHAPE & FOCUS (Lessons 3, 8, 9, 10, 12, 14): asking questions, linking arguments, shifting focus with passives/causatives, and combining ideas with relative or participle clauses.

4. TONE & PRECISION (Lessons 7, 15): comparing persuasively, hedging claims, and spotlighting key ideas with clefts or inversion.

Pattern:

TIME: tenses (L1) · narrative layers (L2) · reported speech (L13)

CHOICE: modals (L4) · conditionals (L5) · wishes & regrets (L6) · gerunds & infinitives (L11)

SHAPE: questions & follow-ups (L3) · linkers (L8) · passive (L9) · causative (L10) · relatives (L12) · participles (L14)

STYLE: comparisons (L7) · hedging, clefts & inversion (L15)

Natural examples:

• Story + reflection in four moves: 'Two years ago I was working at a small clinic (TIME — L2) when my mentor encouraged me to apply for a fellowship (TIME/CHOICE — L13/L11). Although the exam was far more demanding than I expected (SHAPE/STYLE — L8/L7), passing it changed my career — and if I hadn't taken that chance, I wouldn't be teaching here today (CHOICE — L5).'

Keep in mind:

→ Accuracy always comes before complexity: a clear, accurate sentence that fits your meaning beats a complicated structure forced into the wrong place.

Rule 2 — The three-step speaking habit and the art of self-repair

Many learners think fluency means speaking fast without ever making a mistake. In reality, even native speakers and experienced professionals start sentences that head down a blind alley. The difference is that confident speakers do not freeze, apologize, or switch back to their first language — they use a smooth self-repair phrase ('What I mean is…', 'Or rather…', 'Let me put that another way…') and keep the message moving.

In speaking assessments and professional life alike, catching and repairing a slip calmly is a sign of high linguistic control.

Pattern:

The 3-step habit: 1. PICTURE the meaning → 2. PICK the right tool (Time / Choice / Shape / Style) → 3. SPEAK the chunk whole

Natural self-repair phrases: What I mean is … · Or rather, … · Let me rephrase that — … · To put it more precisely, …

Natural examples:

• Repairing a tense slip mid-sentence: 'I have seen him yesterday — or rather, I saw him yesterday afternoon outside the library.'

• Repairing a conditional slip: 'If I would have known — sorry, if I had known about the traffic, I would have taken the train.'

• Sharpening an idea: 'The new schedule is better — or to put it more precisely, it gives working students far more flexibility.'

Keep in mind:

→ Never stop dead in silence when you notice a grammar slip. Either repair it in one smooth breath with 'or rather…' or keep moving forward so your listener never loses the thread of your message.

Part 3 · See the Difference

Freezing on a mistake vs repairing like a confident speaker

Compare how two speakers handle the exact same mid-sentence grammar slip during a speaking task:

Freezing (loses fluency)

Natural self-repair (shows control)

Why the repair works

'Despite of the rain… uh… no, wait… although rain… sorry, I forgot the word…'

'Despite the heavy rain — or rather, although it was raining heavily — the outdoor concert went ahead.'

Speaker A panics over a preposition and loses the listener. Speaker B pivots smoothly with 'or rather', repairs the structure in stride, and finishes the thought with authority.

Knowing a rule on paper vs owning it under real-time pressure

You already recognize all sixteen grammar areas when you read them quietly. The four-round speaking workout below trains your brain to summon those same patterns on your feet while your attention is focused on communicating a real idea.

Part 4 · Practice the Pattern

A. Complete each sentence with the most natural form, then say it aloud.

1. Repair the mistake and name the rule: 'I have finished my university degree in 2022.'

2. Repair the mistake and name the rule: 'If the flight will be delayed tomorrow, we will call the hotel.'

3. Repair the mistake in two ways (despite / although): 'Despite of the cold wind, we walked to the summit.'

4. Repair the mistake and name the verb pattern: 'My supervisor suggested me to attend the workshop.'

5. Repair the word order: 'Never I have felt so proud of our team.'

6. Repair the verb form after 'to': 'We really look forward to host your delegation next month.'

B. Repair, transform, or build the sentence so the meaning is clear.

1. Compress using a participle opening: 'Because he had not slept the night before, he made several small calculation errors.'

2. Report this sentence in two ways (using 'told' and 'reassured'): '"Don't worry about the deadline," she said to me.'

3. Strengthen this flat comparison using 'far', a comparative, and a 'because' reason: 'Practising out loud is better than silent reading.'

4. Rewrite as a formal passive announcement: 'The committee has changed tomorrow's examination schedule.'

5. Hedge this sweeping claim so it sounds measured: 'This new teaching method is the best for every learner.'

6. Turn this direct question into a polite indirect question: 'What time does tomorrow's rehearsal start?'

Part 5 · Pair Speaking

Speak with a partner

Run the 'Four-Round Conversation Circuit' with your partner. In each round, speak for one full minute on the prompt while deliberately weaving in the target grammar family. Your partner listens, asks one follow-up question, and notes which structures they heard.

• Round 1 — Story & Time (Lessons 1, 2, 14): Tell the story of a challenge or problem you overcame, using narrative tenses and one participle opening.

• Round 2 — Choice & Advice (Lessons 4, 5, 6): Advise a friend who is torn between two career paths or cities, using modals, conditionals, and 'If I were you / I'd rather'.

• Round 3 — Report & Focus (Lessons 9, 10, 12, 13): Summarize a recent change or conversation at school, work, or in your city, using passives, reporting verbs, and relative clauses.

• Round 4 — Persuade & Spotlight (Lessons 7, 8, 15): Argue for one practical improvement in your community, using comparisons, concession linkers, hedging, and a cleft sentence.

How it sounds in conversation:

A (Round 4): Although expanding our public library hours would require extra staffing, it is by far the most helpful step we could take for students. What many learners lack at home is a quiet desk with reliable lighting...

B: If the library stayed open until nine, how do you think students would manage transport home in winter?

Your conversation goal: Four one-minute rounds per pair: each round delivered without notes, with the target structures counted aloud and at least one self-repair noted by the listener.

What makes this conversation work:

✓ summons structures from the target grammar family naturally in each round

✓ uses self-repair phrases smoothly if a slip occurs rather than stopping

✓ connects ideas with clear signposts and reasons

✓ responds to the partner's follow-up question with confidence and accuracy

Part 6 · Say It with Greater Precision

At your highest level of spoken control, different grammar families work together inside a single breath — combining a conditional with reported speech, or opening an argument with an inversion and closing it with a cleft.

From clear accuracy to richer expression

Make the core pattern automatic:

• Go back to any earlier lesson where an exercise made you hesitate and speak those corrected sentences aloud three times without looking at the page.

• Create four personal anchor sentences — one each for Time, Choice, Shape, and Style — about your own life goals this year.

Add nuance, detail, and sharper focus:

• Combine two course structures smoothly inside one sentence: 'Had I known that the application deadline had been brought forward, I would have had my transcripts translated a week earlier.'

• Pace your rhetorical style deliberately across a two-minute talk: open with a concrete story, hedge your central prediction, and land your conclusion with a crisp cleft sentence.

• Keep three natural self-repair and refinement phrases on the tip of your tongue: 'What I mean is…', 'Let me rephrase that…', and 'Or to put it more precisely…'.

Part 7 · Real Talk Challenge

Your speaking challenge

Prepare: Take one minute to plan your culminating two-minute talk on 'How my communication has changed — and where I am heading next.' Write down only three brief keyword lines: (1) Past story (where you started and what turning point changed your approach), (2) Present habits & choices (what you do differently now and why), and (3) Future goal (what you plan to achieve next and what it will take). Choose two precision structures (such as a mixed conditional, a non-defining relative clause, or a cleft) to weave in.

Speak without reading: Two-minute culminating challenge: Speak for two minutes on 'How I have grown as a speaker — and what comes next.' Tell a concrete story from your past, explain a decision that helped you improve, and state your next goal, using structures from at least six different lessons in this course. Then exchange two follow-up questions with your partner — just as you will in the Final Speaking Assessment.

Model response — speak first, then compare

Two years ago, I used to avoid speaking English in group meetings because I was afraid of making mistakes — while others were sharing their ideas, I would translate every sentence in my head until the moment had passed. Joining a weekly speaking circle, which a colleague recommended to me, was the turning point that changed that habit. Within a month, I had met partners who corrected me encouragingly, and I realised that communication is about clarity, not perfection. Since then, I've been practising aloud almost every day, and my supervisor has noticed the difference. Next spring I'm going to take the TOEFL exam so that I can apply for a graduate programme. If I keep building one small habit at a time, the score will take care of itself. What matters most to me now is staying calm under pressure — and that comes only from using my voice every day.

Partner listening checklist:

✓ uses a wide range of course structures (at least six lessons represented) accurately and naturally

✓ moves smoothly from past narrative to present reflection to future goal

✓ includes at least one precision or emphasis structure (relative clause, conditional, hedge, or cleft)

✓ maintains confident, continuous delivery and handles follow-up questions or self-repair smoothly

Part 8 · Review and Self-Check

Core insights to carry with you:

• All sixteen lessons serve four practical communication jobs: Time, Choice, Sentence Shape, and Style.

• Follow the three-step speaking habit: picture the meaning → pick the structure → speak the phrase whole.

• When you notice a slip in real conversation, use a natural repair phrase ('What I mean is…', 'Or rather…') and keep your message moving.

Common traps to avoid:

→ Never sacrifice clarity just to show off a complicated structure — natural accuracy always comes first.

→ Never freeze in silence after a small slip — repair calmly with 'or rather…' and continue.

Close the book and try this from memory:

• Name the four communication jobs of grammar and give one example sentence of your own for each job.

• Speak for 60 seconds about a goal for next year, deliberately including one conditional, one relative clause, and one cleft sentence.

Self-check — can you do this now?

☐ I can combine grammar patterns from across the course naturally in a two-minute unscripted talk.

☐ I can answer unexpected follow-up questions and self-repair smoothly without losing confidence.

If a box is unticked: return to Part 2 · The Simple Rule for this lesson, redo the matching practice item, and check Formula Book card 16 in Appendix 1 before you move on.

Quick answers

Practice A: 1. I finished my university degree in 2022. ('in 2022' is a finished past time → past simple) · 2. If the flight is delayed tomorrow, we will call the hotel. (ordinary future condition → present simple after 'if') · 3. Despite the cold wind, we walked to the summit. / Although the wind was cold, we walked to the summit. · 4. My supervisor suggested attending the workshop. / …suggested that I attend the workshop. ('suggest' takes -ing or a that-clause, never 'me to') · 5. Never have I felt so proud of our team. (negative opener triggers auxiliary + subject inversion) · 6. We really look forward to hosting your delegation next month. ('to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition → verb-ing)

Practice B: 1. Not having slept the night before, he made several small calculation errors. · 2. She told me not to worry about the deadline. / She reassured me that I didn't need to worry about the deadline. · 3. answers vary (e.g. 'Practising out loud is far more effective than silent reading because it trains your mouth and ear to work together in real time.') · 4. Tomorrow's examination schedule has been changed (by the committee). · 5. This new teaching method may well be one of the most effective for many learners. / This new teaching method tends to work very well for most learners. (answers vary) · 6. Could you tell me what time tomorrow's rehearsal starts? / Do you know what time tomorrow's rehearsal starts?

FINAL ASSESSMENT

Part 1: Grammar knowledge · Part 2: Independent speaking task

Part 1 — Grammar knowledge (30 questions · suggested time: 35 minutes)

Section A — Complete the sentences. (12 questions)

1. I __________ (live) here since 2020.

2. When I got home, my family __________ (already / have) dinner.

3. If it __________ (be) sunny tomorrow, we'll go to the lake.

4. I wish I __________ (not/say) that yesterday.

5. The meeting __________ (cancel) yesterday afternoon.

6. You look exhausted — you __________ (must / work) all night. (past deduction)

7. She avoided __________ (make) any promises.

8. The teacher made us __________ (rewrite) the essay.

9. This is the most __________ (challenge) course I've ever taken.

10. __________ (warn) about the storm, the fishermen stayed ashore.

11. He suggested __________ (leave) before the traffic.

12. Not only __________ (she / apologise), but she also offered a refund.

Section B — Rewrite or transform. (10 questions)

13. Report: 'I'll help you tomorrow,' he said.

14. Report: 'Where did you buy it?' (She asked me…)

15. Polite question: 'When does the shop close?'

16. Third conditional: 'He didn't revise, so he failed.'

17. Passive (formal): 'Someone has stolen the documents.'

18. Cleft (focus the manager): 'The manager approved the plan.'

19. Causative: 'I paid someone to fix the roof.'

20. Inversion: 'She had rarely felt so confident.'

21. Combine with although: 'The task was difficult. They finished it.'

22. Combine with a participle: 'Because he had studied hard, he passed easily.'

Section C — Use and communication. (8 questions)

23. Choose: He (mustn't / can't) be at home — his car is gone.

24. Complete with a linker: __________ being expensive, the course is worth it.

25. Hedge the claim: 'This method is the best.' (may well / probably)

26. Compare with nuance: 'Option A is better than Option B.' (use far + give a reason frame)

27. Correct: 'The book what I read was amazing.'

28. Complete: The more you practise, the __________ (confident) you become.

29. Report advice: 'You should apply early,' she said. (She advised…)

30. Complete with the right pattern: I look forward to __________ (meet) you.

Stop here until you have completed all 30 items. The answer key is in Appendix 5.

Accept alternative answers where the exercise allows them (e.g. 'may well' / 'probably' / 'is likely to' for hedging). The Diagnostic Test is a broad starting snapshot, not a parallel form of this 30-item assessment. Do not compare the raw grammar totals as a measure of gain; compare your four speaking-rubric criterion scores instead.

FINAL ASSESSMENT — PART 2

Independent speaking task and evaluation

Speaking task (2 minutes to prepare · 2 minutes to speak, then follow-up exchange)

Speak on ONE of the following topics:

• A decision that changed your life — and what you would do differently today.

• One change that would improve education or work in your country.

• A person who influenced you, and the advice they gave you.

After your talk, a partner asks two follow-up questions. Answer them, then ask one relevant question in return. If you get stuck, repair and continue.

You may make brief notes during the preparation time. Speak without reading a script.

Evaluation rubric

Criterion

4 — Strong

3 — Good

2 — Developing

1 — Beginning

Grammatical accuracy

structures are consistently accurate; occasional slips do not affect meaning

generally accurate; some errors, meaning always clear

frequent errors; meaning sometimes unclear

errors dominate; meaning often unclear

Appropriate structure selection

wide range used naturally (tenses, conditionals, linkers, hedging…) for the intended meaning

good range; choices usually match the meaning

limited range; some structures forced or inappropriate

basic structures only; frequent wrong choices

Clarity

ideas well organised and easy to follow; effective linking

clear overall; some linking

ideas loosely connected; hard to follow at times

ideas listed without clear connection

Successful communication

message fully delivered; natural delivery, relevant follow-up exchange and self-repair

message delivered; answers and asks relevant follow-ups, with some hesitation

message partly delivered; responses are limited or pauses are long

message largely not delivered; little response to questions

Score: ____ / 16 Compare each criterion with your recorded Diagnostic speaking score.

Personal error analysis and improvement plan

Copy every error you made in the Final Assessment (written and spoken) into the table. An error that is analysed is halfway to being fixed.

My error

Correct form

Why it happened (rule I forgot)

My fix — where I will practise it

My next three goals:

1. ________________________________________________________________

2. ________________________________________________________________

3. ________________________________________________________________

Remember: improvement is measured by what you can do in speech — not by pages completed. Record yourself speaking for two minutes on the same topic in a month, and listen to the difference.

APPENDIX 1 · GRAMMAR FORMULA BOOK

Sixteen cards — one per lesson. Review with this book closed first.

Card 1 — Tenses for Real Communication

Present simple = facts & habits · Present continuous = around now

Past simple = finished time · Present perfect = connected to now

going to = plan · will = decision/prediction · present continuous = arrangement

Card 2 — Telling Stories

Past continuous = the scene · past simple = the events · past perfect = the earlier past

when + past simple · while + past continuous · by the time + past perfect before past simple

Shape: background → events (First… Then…) → ending/reflection

Card 3 — Questions and Follow-ups

Wh- + auxiliary + subject + verb · Yes/No: auxiliary + subject + verb

Indirect: question word + subject + verb (no inversion) — 'Do you know where the bank is?'

Follow-ups keep conversations alive: 'Really? What happened next? How about you?'

Card 4 — Modal Verbs

Modal + base verb: can/could = ability · may/could = permission · must/have to = obligation · should = advice · might = possibility

must be = certainly (positive) · might be = possible · can't be = certainly not

mustn't = prohibition ≠ can't (deduction) · Would you mind + -ing?

Card 5 — Conditionals

Zero: If + present, present · First: If + present, will + verb

Second: If + past, would + verb · Third: If + past perfect, would have + participle

Mixed: If + past perfect, would + verb · unless = if not · ordinary future if-clause: present simple

Card 6 — Wishes and Regrets

wish + past simple = present wish · wish + past perfect = past regret

wish + would = complaint/request · If only…! = strong emotion

would rather + base (me) / + past (someone else) · It's (high) time + past

Card 7 — Comparisons

comparative + than (compare two) · superlative (extreme in a group) · as + adj + as

the + comparative, the + comparative · comparative + and + comparative

far / much / slightly / by far + comparison · comparisons persuade with reasons

Card 8 — Linking and Arguments

although + clause · despite / in spite of + noun or -ing · however = new sentence

because + clause · because of + noun · therefore / as a result = consequence

Argument skeleton: POINT → REASON → EXAMPLE → SUMMARY

Card 9 — Passive Voice

be + past participle (tense lives in 'be'): is done · was done · will be done · has been done · must be done

Use: result matters · doer unknown/obvious/general · objective tone

It is said that … = He is said to …

Card 10 — Causative Structures

have/get + object + participle = arrange a service (or: something happened to me)

make + person + base (force) · let + base (allow) · have + base (instruct) · get + to (persuade)

'get' keeps 'to' — the other three don't.

Card 11 — Gerunds and Infinitives

enjoy/avoid/mind/suggest/keep + -ing · decide/hope/plan/promise/refuse + to

remember/forget/stop/try: -ing = earlier action · to = later action

Preposition + -ing — including 'to' in look forward to / be used to

Card 12 — Relative Clauses

who (people) · which (things) · that (both) · whose · where — object pronouns can drop

Defining = no commas (identifies) · Non-defining = commas (extra detail, no 'that')

Reduced: 'the man (who is) standing there' — only drop who is / which was

Card 13 — Reported Speech

Backshift one tense: present → past → past perfect · will → would · can → could

ask + if/whether or question word + statement order · told/asked + person + to

say (+ that) vs tell (+ person) · time words shift: tomorrow → the next day

Card 14 — Participles

-ing adjective = causes feeling · -ed adjective = feels it (boring lecture / bored class)

Participle clause: 'Having finished, she left.' — subject must match the main clause

Frames: Given… / Considering… / With + noun + -ing

Card 15 — Hedging, Emphasis, Inversion

Hedge: may well / might / tend to / it could be argued that …

Cleft: It was X that … / What I need is … · do-emphasis: 'I do believe…'

Inversion after negative openers: Never have I… / Not only did… / Only then did…

Card 16 — Grammar in Real Conversation

Four jobs: TIME (tenses, reported) · CHOICE (modals, conditionals, wishes) · SHAPE (questions, linkers, relatives, passives) · STYLE (comparison, hedging, emphasis)

Think meaning → choose structure → say it whole

Accuracy first, then range; repair and continue: 'What I mean is…'

APPENDIX 2 · COMMON ERRORS AND CORRECTIONS GUIDE

Thirty errors that mark learners — and the fix for each

✗ Error

✓ Correction

Why

I have seen him yesterday.

I saw him yesterday.

finished time needs past simple

I am knowing the answer.

I know the answer.

state verbs take simple forms

She is more taller than me.

She is taller than me.

no double comparatives

This is better then that.

This is better than that.

than (comparison) not then (time)

If it will rain, we'll stay.

If it rains, we'll stay.

present simple in an ordinary future condition

If I would have known…

If I had known…

third conditional: if + past perfect

I wish I have more time.

I wish I had more time.

wish + past for unreal present

I'd rather you don't smoke.

I'd rather you didn't smoke.

would rather + subject + past

It's time we will go.

It's time we went.

it's time + past (already late)

Despite of the cost…

Despite the cost… / In spite of the cost…

no 'despite of'

Although the cost, we bought it.

Despite the cost, we bought it.

although + clause; despite + noun

Do you know where is the bank?

Do you know where the bank is?

indirect questions use statement order

Did she called you?

Did she call you?

base verb after did

He said me that he was tired.

He told me that he was tired.

tell + person; say + that

She suggested me to wait.

She suggested waiting.

suggest + -ing (or that + clause)

I look forward to meet you.

I look forward to meeting you.

'to' here is a preposition

I enjoy to read.

I enjoy reading.

enjoy + -ing

He made me to wait.

He made me wait.

make + person + base verb

I will get my car to repair.

I will get my car repaired.

have/get + object + participle

The house was builted in 1990.

The house was built in 1990.

past participle of build = built

My phone was stolen by me.

I lost my phone.

active is clearer for your own actions

The book what I read…

The book (that) I read…

no 'what' as a relative pronoun

My mother, that lives…

My mother, who lives…

'that' is not used after commas

Never I have seen such a mess.

Never have I seen such a mess.

inversion after negative openers

He mustn't be at home.

He can't be at home.

can't = deduction; mustn't = prohibition

Would you mind to open the window?

Would you mind opening the window?

mind + -ing

I am very interesting in history.

I am very interested in history.

-ed = feels; -ing = causes

Opening the window, the room was cold.

Opening the window, I felt the cold.

participle subject must match

He denied to break it.

He denied breaking it.

deny + -ing

Unless you don't hurry…

Unless you hurry…

'unless' already means 'if not'

APPENDIX 3 · ESSENTIAL SENTENCE PATTERNS FOR SPEAKING

Build answers from these skeletons until they are automatic

Function

Patterns

Experience

I have (never) … · One experience that changed me was …

Story

First … Then … After that … Suddenly … Finally …

Opinion

I believe that … because … · From my point of view …

Reason

This is mainly because … · The main reason is that …

Example

For instance … · A good example of this is …

Contrast

Although …, … · Despite + noun/-ing … · On the other hand …

Concession

It is true that …; nevertheless … · Admittedly …; even so …

Result

As a result … · This means that … · Consequently …

Hedged claim

It could be argued that … · … may well … · … tend(s) to …

Emphasis

It is … that … · What I mean is … · I do believe …

Advice

If I were you, I'd … · You might want to … · It might be worth …

Regret

I wish I had … · If only I had … · What I should have done was …

Preference

I'd rather … than … · I prefer … to … · If I had to choose, I'd …

Prediction

In the future, … will probably … · … is likely to …

Polite request

Would you mind …-ing? · Could I possibly …? · I was wondering if …

Reporting

He said (that) … · She pointed out that … · They warned me not to …

Description

…, who/which … · The person who … · …, which means that …

Comparison

… is far more … than … · The more …, the more … · … is by far the most …

Process

First, … is done; then … is … · Having been …, … · … is then …

Summary

To sum up … · All in all … · The point I want to make is …

Self-repair

What I mean is … · Let me rephrase that … · Or rather …

Ending

That's why … · This taught me that … · Looking ahead, I plan to …

Tick honestly: ✓ = I can do this in speech · ~ = almost · ✗ = not yet

Speaking self-assessment

Record yourself for two minutes (any topic) and rate yourself with the Final Assessment rubric. Repeat after one month and compare the recordings — that is your true progress.

Lesson

Can-do statement

Before course

After Lesson 16

Lesson 1

I can talk about habits, current situations and past experiences accurately.

Lesson 2

Lesson 3

Lesson 4

Lesson 14

APPENDIX 5 · COMPLETE ANSWER KEY

All exercises, review tests and the final assessment

Alternative answers are accepted where the exercise allows them. Speaking tasks are evaluated with the success criteria and rubric — not with rigid model answers.

Diagnostic

A. 1. saw · 2. has worked / has been working · 3. was cooking · 4. had worked / had been working; 'worked' is also possible with before · 5. boils · 6. were building · 7. have lost · 8. went · 9. have read · 10. had already left

B. 1. rains · 2. knew · 3. repairing / to be repaired · 4. was written · 5. leaving · 6. the station is · 7. who / that · 8. didn't smoke · 9. more intelligent · 10. did she finish

C. 1. can't · 2. Despite · 3. where I lived / where I live (if still true) · 4. may / might / could · 5. had / got

Practice B: 1. I finished my assignment last night. ('last night' is a finished time) · 2. She knows three foreign languages. ('know' is a state verb) · 3. have you known · 4. I'm going to study medicine next year.

No, not at all. / Of course not — take your time. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'You should drink some water and rest your eyes. You might also want to step outside for some fresh air.')

If I have free time tonight, I will review the vocabulary. · 5. answers vary (e.g. 'If I were you, I wouldn't resign until I had a signed offer in hand.') · 6. answers vary

Practising with a partner is far better than studying alone because you have to respond in real time. I have always been very interested in architectural history. · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Having had a cup of green tea, I sat down to read Lesson 14.')

Practice A: 1. Never · 2. did she pass · 3. did I understand · 4. suggests (or: suggest) · 5. the detailed budget · 6. tend

Never have I seen such a busy market. · 5. answers vary (e.g. Teammate: 'Could I have two more days on the report?' / Director: 'I was wondering if it might be possible to extend the deadline by two days so we can verify the final figures.') · 6. answers vary (e.g. 'Not only does my mentor listen patiently, but she also gives practical advice.')

Lesson 16

Practice A: 1. I finished my university degree in 2022. ('in 2022' is a finished past time → past simple) · 2. If the flight is delayed tomorrow, we will call the hotel. (ordinary future condition → present simple after 'if') · 3. Despite the cold wind, we walked to the summit. / Although the wind was cold, we walked to the summit. · 4. My supervisor suggested attending the workshop. / …suggested that I attend the workshop. ('suggest' takes -ing or a that-clause, never 'me to') · 5. Never have I felt so proud of our team. (negative opener triggers auxiliary + subject inversion) · 6. We really look forward to hosting your delegation next month. ('to' in 'look forward to' is a preposition → verb-ing)

Practice B: 1. Not having slept the night before, he made several small calculation errors. · 2. She told me not to worry about the deadline. / She reassured me that I didn't need to worry about the deadline. · 3. answers vary (e.g. 'Practising out loud is far more effective than silent reading because it trains your mouth and ear to work together in real time.') · 4. Tomorrow's examination schedule has been changed (by the committee). · 5. This new teaching method may well be one of the most effective for many learners. / This new teaching method tends to work very well for most learners. (answers vary) · 6. Could you tell me what time tomorrow's rehearsal starts? / Do you know what time tomorrow's rehearsal starts?
